<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 23 Oct 2026 00:48:10 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Central Bank inquiry made ‘fundamental errors’ in former PTSB chief tracker mortgage case]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:55:20 +0000A tribunal has confirmed that former PTSB chief executive David Guinane has won an appeal against a Central Bank of Ireland inquiry sanctioning him for a role played in the State’s tracker mortgage scandal.

The Irish Financial Services Appeals Tribunal (Ifsat) said that the sole inquiry member, Peter Hinchliffe, made errors of law that were so fundamental that they negated his decision last year that Guinane be fined €80,000 and reprimanded.

The tribunal concluded in a decision published on Thursday that Hinchliffe “erred in law”, acted beyond what was established by case law elsewhere, “failed to give fair notice of certain issues”, and “failed to give reasons for his decision”.

“Moreover, it held that the errors of law in the inquiry decision were manifest from the text and were fundamental so as to deprive the decision of its basis,” said the tribunal, chaired by chaired by former Supreme Court judge John MacMenamin.

Its conclusion still needs to be confirmed by the High Court. The Central Bank said it does not plan to appeal it.

The Irish Times first reported on the conclusion of the appeal last month.

Former PTSB chief wins appeal over tracker mortgage sanction

“This deeply flawed process, which has cost millions in taxpayer funds, has had a profound effect on my family and on my career,” said Guinane in a statement on Thursday afternoon.

“With this now-discredited allegation, the Central Bank tried to single me out as a scapegoat. It is extraordinary that I was the only individual to be subject to a formal inquiry in respect of the tracker issue.”

Ifsat said that the Central Bank should pay Guinane’s legal costs for the inquiry and appeal, including his €5,000 appeal fee.

It rejected an application by PTSB, a notice party in the case, for costs. PTSB paid a €21 million fine in 2019 for its role in the industry-wide tracker mortgage scandal.

Hinchliffe emphasised last year there was “no finding of dishonesty against Mr Guinane” and that he “did not form an intention to harm or take advantage of customers”. Guinane was also entitled to receive better support from within the wider Irish Life & Permanent Group, of which PTSB was a part at the time, he added.

The inquiry centred on a special condition in some PTSB tracker mortgages offered during the pre-crash property boom. This required customers who moved for a period to a fixed rate to instruct the bank afterwards to put them back on a tracker rate or another fixed product. Otherwise, they would default to a standard variable rate.

The ambiguous wording of the condition led to questions in early 2009 about whether a customer opting to go back on to a tracker rate was entitled to their original margin over the European Central Bank rate, or a higher margin then on offer from PTSB.

The bank adopted a strategy in January 2009, on the basis of legal advice, to only put customers who requested the original rate – or complained – on the more favourable rate. The Central Bank said Guinane signed off on the strategy when he responded to the plan, when advanced by a colleague via email in January 2009, with the words, “okay to that”.

Guinane testified during an inquiry hearing in early 2024 that while he did not remember events surrounding the decision, he understood the email to mean – based on having reviewed documents – that “any customer” coming out of the fixed rate would “go back to their original rate”. The email only contained a summary of the legal advice.

The grounds for the Central Bank’s decision to hold the inquiry were that Guinane knew and understood the strategy.

However, Ifsat said Hinchliffe reframed the allegation by removing “those critical elements of knowledge and approval”.

Instead, Hinchliffe criticised Guinane’s “failure” to ask certain questions, to make follow-up enquiries, or to take other steps which might have shown him what was happening to PTSB customers.

“The meaning of the allegation, as originally notified to the appellant was fundamentally altered in the ultimate decision,” Ifsat said.

The Ifsat decision raises questions about whether the Central Bank will still go after other bankers suspected of having played a role in the tracker mortgage scandal.

Ifsat’s conclusion marks another major setback for the regulator’s post-crisis vetting and enforcement activities.

Ifsat was previously highly critical in 2024 of a Central Bank refusal to approve a board nominee for a fund, saying the decision-making process was “flawed” and denied the individual fair procedures “at every stage”.

The Central Bank was also found in a High Court ruling, published in April, to have badly handled an enforcement investigation into a funds industry executive, saying it was “irretrievably tainted” by errors. The bank committed to learning lessons and changing procedures as a result of both cases.

]]>sam boal<![CDATA[Avant Money profits rise 21% in first nine months of 2026 as loan book expands]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/avant-money-profits-rise-21-in-first-nine-months-of-2026-as-loan-book-expands/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/avant-money-profits-rise-21-in-first-nine-months-of-2026-as-loan-book-expands/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 06:43:16 +0000Avant Money, the Irish unit of Spanish banking group Bankinter, saw its net profit for the first nine months of the year rise 21 per cent as its loans grew at pace, driven by mortgages.

Net profit rose to €41 million, even after setting aside €17 million for problem loans and other provisions, according to a presentation from Bankinter that accompanied its latest quarterly results.

A spokesman clarified that the charge relates to the Irish lenders’ year-to-date credit impairment charge across cards, loans and mortgages.

“The overall cost of risk remains in line with our expectations at approximately 46 basis points, compared with 44 basis points in the same period last year,” he said. “The impairment charge is consistent with a growing lending portfolio.”

One basis point equates to 0.01 of a percentage point.

Denis McGoldrick, an analyst with Goodbody, highlighted that the lender’s “asset quality remains strong, with the Irish [non-performing loan] ratio of just 0.3 per cent”.

The company’s loan book rose by 26 per cent on the year to €5.6 billion at the end of September. The presentation did not give a breakdown of Irish deposits. Avant officially launched a deposit offering in February, months after carrying out a soft launch of savings products.

The company, led by chief executive Niall Corbett, became a branch of Madrid-headquartered Bankinter last year, allowing it to venture into deposit gathering with the benefit of the group’s Spanish licence.

Avant Money builds up €100m deposit book in first half after entry into savings market

Bankinter has previously said it expected the Irish loan book would be almost fully funded by local deposits within eight years of the launch of savings products.

“The strategic objective is increasingly clear: management expects Ireland to finance the incremental growth of its own loan book, progressively creating a more balanced local loan-to-deposit position rather than relying on group funding,” said McGoldrick.

“Alongside deposits, the bank continues to build out its digital banking proposition, with the broader strategy focused on acquiring customers and developing longer-term relationships rather than competing solely on deposit pricing.”

Avant’s interest income increased 21 per cent for the nine months to €103 million.

Mortgage activity also remains supportive, with Ireland and Portugal together accounting for around half of group mortgage origination outside Spain. Management characterised Ireland as continuing to gain scale while maintaining strong profitability and asset quality.

The wider Bankinter group reported 11 per cent growth in net profit for the nine months, to €901 million.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[Global stocks dip after AI boom stalls and motor industry slows ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/global-stocks-slump-as-ai-boom-proves-dangerous-game-and-motor-industry-slows-down/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/global-stocks-slump-as-ai-boom-proves-dangerous-game-and-motor-industry-slows-down/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:58:52 +0000Global stocks slumped on Thursday as industry old and new suffered pullbacks in trader confidence. The artificial intelligence (AI) boom in the US is proving to be a dangerous game for investors worried about recent filings from Meta, while the motor industry in Britain dragged its stock indices into the red.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share index fell 1.86 per cent to close at 14,026.41, following sizeable drops in the banking sector in particular and little upward movement elsewhere.

AIB saw its stock decrease 4.58 per cent to €10.64 a share, while rival Bank of Ireland fared only slightly better, down 3.81 per cent to close at €18.04 on the day it announced higher interest rates to its fixed-term savings deposit account. Permanent TSB, meanwhile, saw no change in its share price.

Elsewhere, building materials specialist group Kingspan fell 3.90 per cent to €91.20 a share, while Ryanair saw its share price slump 2.59 per cent to close at €22.96.

Nutrition business Kerry Group jumped in share price, up 6.07 per cent to close at €99.60 a share. Its chief executive said earlier in the day the surge in demand for weight loss medications was helping its business to boom.

London

Stocks in London fell into the red by the close of markets, with the British motor industry slowing down so much that not even a strong showing from real estate companies could drive its stock indices into positive returns.

London’s blue-chip FTSE 100 dipped 0.26, while its mid-cap FTSE 250 index fell 0.93 by the end of trading hours.

Aston Martin’s share price decreased 7.21 per cent as the fallout from legal disputes continues to affect investor confidence that the car brand is a safe bet, while ongoing supply chain issues are also blamed by some. Rolls-Royce fell 5.11 per cent as well to its lowest share price in recent weeks as a technical correction on its valuation pulled its stock lower.

Meanwhile, the online real estate company Rightmove was up 3.63 per cent as buy-backs keep its stock on a consistently upward trajectory.

Europe

Elsewhere in Europe, stock indices were not much better, following poor results from the Continent’s luxury goods and energy industries, leading investors to look for safer bets in the telecommunications and pharmaceutical sectors.

The blue-chip Euro Stoxx 50 index closed 1.96 per cent lower on Thursday, with the mid-cap Stoxx 600 index fairly slightly better, down 1.05 per cent at the end of trading.

Luxury goods giant Hermes saw its share price fall after investors lost confidence that the French house can truly compete with Chinese competitors – its third-quarter revenue fell short of analysts’ forecasts and represented the lowest quarterly growth rate it has seen since early 2020.

Meanwhile, German multinational software company SAP’s share price rose after it announced a 12 per cent jump in revenue, which the company largely attributed to increased demand for services supported by AI.

New York

Stocks on Wall Street slid into the negative by midday New York time, as earnings reports from big tech companies in the US rattled investors’ confidence and continued warfare between the US and Iran shot oil prices up.

The Nasdaq index slumped nearly 2.5 per cent, while the S&P 500 fell about 1.25 per cent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped some 0.2 per cent before noon.

Strikes in Saudi Arabia and around the Gulf drove the price of Brent crude oil, the industry benchmark, to $112 – the highest price since May. This only stoked many traders’ inflation worries and pushed the prospect of peace in the Middle East farther away.

Companies at the coalface of AI expansion pulled down many stock indices as investors grew wary of the new technology’s ability to bring in big returns.

Meta reported a sizeable decline in cash flow on Wednesday and indicated it would struggle to fund data centre construction on its current path, leading the company to open more than 5 per cent down at the start of trading hours Thursday. – Additional reporting: The New York Times.

]]>Christophe Petit Tesson<![CDATA[Fitzwilliam Hotel in Dublin checks in again with a profit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/fitzwilliam-hotel-in-dublin-checks-in-again-with-a-profit/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/fitzwilliam-hotel-in-dublin-checks-in-again-with-a-profit/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 17:07:16 +0000The company behind the five-star Fitzwilliam Hotel in Dublin returned to profit last year, latest accounts show.

Filings for Ampleforth Ltd show that it made a profit of €1.6 million in the year to the end of December 2025. This marked a turnaround on the previous year when the company recorded a loss of €1.3 million.

Turnover rose by 10 per cent to €22.2 million as the business concluded a three-year refurbishment of the hotel in the first half of the year.

“The programme, which incorporated both bedrooms and common areas, has enhanced the guest experience and improved the energy efficiency of the building,” the directors’ report states.

“Trading performance has strengthened during the year, with improved occupancy and room yield reflecting the enhanced offering and the return to full inventory availability.”

The company’s staff numbers declined to 200 from 211 a year earlier, while its total payroll costs reduced by 18.5 per cent to €7.5 million.

Ampleforth is controlled by Michael Holland.

]]>James Newton<![CDATA[Bank of Ireland and PTSB raise interest rates on products for first time since June ECB hike ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/bank-of-ireland-and-ptsb-raise-interest-rates-on-products-for-first-time-since-june-ecb-hike/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/bank-of-ireland-and-ptsb-raise-interest-rates-on-products-for-first-time-since-june-ecb-hike/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 10:02:16 +0000Bank of Ireland and PTSB have raised the interest rates on some of their fixed-rate products on Thursday, making them the first mainstream domestic Irish banks to do so since the European Central Bank (ECB) began raising rates in recent months.

Bank of Ireland increased the interest rate on some of its fixed-term savings deposit accounts, while PTSB has raised fixed mortgage rates. The changes are effective from today, the banks said.

They follow recent moves by non-bank lenders, such as Nua Money, the newest mortgage lender to establish itself in the State, as well as ICS Mortgages, recently acquired by Pepper Advantage.

It comes weeks after the ECB increased its interest rates by 0.25 per cent in early September. The second time it has done so since June, it is expected by many economists to increase rates again in December.

Bank of Ireland said it has increased its six- and 12-month advantage fixed-term deposit savings rate by 0.25 per cent each and its 18-month offer by 0.5 per cent, the bank announced Wednesday morning.

Customers of any scheme can access “up to 25 per cent of their deposited funds during the term, providing flexibility should they need access to some of their savings”, it added.

“Existing fixed-term deposit customers will continue to earn interest at their existing rate until the end of their current term,” the company said in a statement.

Meanwhile, PTSB has raised its four-year fixed rate mortgage 0.2 per cent – the lowest of all its increases. The bank increased its seven-year fixed rate, three-year higher value mortgage, and three-year green mortgage by 0.25 per cent each, and its five- and three-year fixed rate mortgage rates by 0.3 per cent, respectively.

Among PTSB’s largest increases on Thursday were its five-year higher value mortgage, five-year green mortgage and five-year green mortgage of more than €250,000 – all by 0.35 per cent.

Bank of Ireland’s director of everyday banking, Carol Meehan, said: “These increases strengthen the returns available across our fixed-term savings range, while giving customers a choice of six-, 12- and 18-month terms and the option of accessing up to 25% of their money during the term.”

]]>Kirill Kudryavtsev<![CDATA[Department not capable of ‘great conspiracy’ to oust Labour Court member, official says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/official-says-department-not-capable-of-mounting-great-conspiracy-to-oust-labour-court-member/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/official-says-department-not-capable-of-mounting-great-conspiracy-to-oust-labour-court-member/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:40:16 +0000A senior civil servant has said the Department of Enterprise could not mount the “great conspiracy” she said had been alleged by a former Labour Court member to oust him from his seat.

“I have to be honest with you, we’re not that good in the State,” the official told the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Tara Coogan, the former head of the department’s industrial relations unit, was giving evidence for a second day on claims of unfair dismissal and other employment rights breaches by Peter DR Murphy, a former business group Ibec nominee to the court.

Coogan told the WRC she felt “unwell” at the suggestion that Murphy was not reappointed because of any connection with a complaint he made against a former Labour Court chairman.

Lawyers acting for Murphy say that when plans emerged to cut back the court, a redundancy situation arose and he was let go with “absolutely no selection process”.

The State says Ibec just didn’t nominate Murphy.

On Monday, the State was directed to produce more documents related to Murphy’s engagements as a Labour Court member between 2005 and 2024, and correspondence coming up to the expiry of his last warrant.

One of the records, a letter dated December 15th, 2023, from then-minister of State at the Department of Enterprise Neale Richmond to Danny McCoy, the head of Ibec, was opened to the WRC on Tuesday.

The letter stated that the minister had received “an analysis by the chairman of the court” to the effect that it had “sufficient resources”.

“It is my intention to suppress the fourth division of the court, reducing the number of divisions from four to three,” the letter continued.

Coogan denied that a redundancy situation had arisen on the Labour Court at the time.

“There is no such thing as a redundancy in the public sector. People move around. If there are vacancies in the system, people aren’t always put in,” she said.

“At this time, Ibec would have confirmed to the department that Murphy was not looking for reappointment,” she went on to say.

She admitted that there was no correspondence stating this.

“There was a lot of meetings in relation to this matter,” Coogan said. “We were informed, and this is orally,” she went on to say.

Lowey said it was hearsay and that his client disputed the assertion.

Coogan said it was relayed to her by an assistant secretary at the department that “Ibec had informed him that Murphy was not seeking reappointment”.

Lowey said the State had produced an “entirely new line of argument that’s not included in any of their three submissions” after being compelled to provide the previously undisclosed 15 December 2023 letter to the WRC.

“It’s grossly unfair, and I’m running out of superlatives to describe the State’s approach to this. It’s outrageous,” he added.

Frances Meenan, for the State, said: “Ibec did not nominate the claimant for reappointment in 2023, it’s as simple as that ... there is absolutely nothing new.”

Under cross-examination, Coogan confirmed that the Labour Court chairman who gave the workflow analysis to Richmond was Kevin Foley.

She denied Foley was involved in the decision to suppress the fourth division of the court, which was a “departmental decision in consultation with the social partners”, she said.

Lowey put it to her that it seemed “arbitrary” that of the two Ibec-nominated warrants set to come to an end in February 2024, the department had sought nominations for only one – the one not held by his client.

“I fully accept that,” Coogan said.

Lowey then put it to her that it was “completely and utterly unreasonable” not to think Ibec would not favour the incumbent in the other role for nomination.

Coogan said Ibec could have nominated Murphy, but the department was “of the view Murphy was not seeking reappointment”.

“When you bring in other matters, it all of a sudden looks like a great conspiracy, but I have to be honest with you, we’re not that good in the State,” Coogan said. “I wouldn’t participate in such a process,” she added.

She confirmed that she was denying that a redundancy situation arose when the court was cut from four divisions to three.

Lowey referred Coogan to a letter from the department’s former head of human resources, Denise Kennedy, on July 31st, 2020.

“My client is being informed by the department that an investigation is going to take place into his bullying and harassment complaint,” Lowey said.

“Can you please confirm for me this letter ... confirms that the parties, having sought to resolve matters, ultimately didn’t and that an investigator would conduct an investigation into his complaint?” Lowey said.

Coogan confirmed the letter stated this but said the department’s current HR chief, Pat Phelan, would be in a better position to give evidence on it: “Things like this, I wouldn’t be aware of them,” she said.

Meenan said the complaint was withdrawn by Murphy. Lowey said this was accepted.

Lowey then put it to her that on the same date, July 31st, 2022, the department had for the first time written to Ibec asking it “not to reappoint [Murphy] but to make three nominations”.

“Isn’t it straining credibility to think these matters aren’t related?” counsel asked.

“That’s absolutely the most ridiculous statement I’ve heard,” Coogan said. She said she knew “nothing” about the complaint. “That assertion is actually making me feel a bit unwell,” she added.

Coogan accepted she was aware of High Court proceedings brought by Murphy in which he secured leave for judicial review of the decision not to reappoint him on October 30th, 2020.

An email confirming a new warrant issued “an hour and 20 minutes” after the High Court ruling, Lowey said.

“Is that a coincidence as well?” he asked Coogan.

Coogan said it would be to ascribe “a remarkable efficiency” to the department to suggest “we would be able to draft warrants and have everything ready at the drop of a hat”.

“We’re not as efficient as that,” she said.

The case is continuing.

Lowey is instructed by McInnes Dunne Murphy for the complainant, Meehan by the Chief State Solicitor’s Office.

]]><![CDATA[Court grants Rathwood injunction over stock held in warehouse]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/22/court-grants-rathwood-injunction-over-stock-held-in-warehouse/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/22/court-grants-rathwood-injunction-over-stock-held-in-warehouse/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:00:58 +0000The Rathwood home and garden furniture company, which recently exited examinership, has obtained a temporary High Court injunction restraining a warehouse company from disposing of furniture which Rathwood says is held for its benefit.

On Thursday, Judge Brian Cregan granted orders to barrister Arthur Cunningham for Rathwood Home and Garden World Ltd, restraining Carlow Warehousing Ltd from disposing of and requiring it to preserve the goods it holds pending further order.

The judge also granted orders permitting the service of proceedings outside the jurisdiction on a company called Paleo Furniture Company Ltd, which the court heard is based in China and has claimed the stock stored with Carlow Warehousing belongs to it. The application was made ex parte, meaning only Rathwood was represented in court.

Earlier this year, on foot of a petition presented by Paleo, along with another creditor of Rathwood, the High Court appointed an examiner to the business. It successfully exited examinership following approval of a survival scheme last July.

In an affidavit, Rathwood managing director Kevin Nolan said that under the terms of that scheme, unsecured creditors were to receive 0.25 per cent of their agreed debts, to include contingent and prospective liabilities due and owing as at the date the dividend is discharged. This was to be in full and final settlement of the creditor’s claims.

Rathwood ends ‘working relationship’ with brothers formerly behind business

The scheme also provided that a separate category of creditor who had retention of title (ROT) status must make any claim to Rathwood within 14 days of the effective date of the scheme. Failure to do so meant the ROT creditor would be treated as an unsecured creditor.

Paleo had ROT status in relation to a debt of some €258,000 while it was also owed some €2.8 million as an unsecured creditor.

Nolan said no claim was submitted by Paleo within the 14-day period or any time after.

As a result, the total dividend payable to Paleo came to €7,724, and Nolan wrote to Paleo on August 19th, 2026, asking for its payment details so the money could be sent on.

Paleo wrote back saying it had not intentionally waived or abandoned its rights to the stored goods and may have legal remedies to protect its interests. It did not accept its ROT rights had been conclusively surrendered.

In a second email reply, Paleo said its position remained that the stock belonged to it.

Paleo agreed to accept the €7,724 but continued to assert its rights over the stock. It also said it did not consent to the removal of the stock from Carlow Warehousing premises.

Nolan said solicitors for Carlow Warehousing, in September 2026, said they would comply with any High Court order but asserted that a lien against Paleo survived and the goods would not be released until ownership was proved.

Nolan said Rathwood requires its stock before the seasonal upswing of activity in the spring of 2027. The company is in a growth phase and would be severely compromised next spring if it is denied access to the stock.

The case returns to court next week.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Why did huge swathes of the internet suddenly go offline yesterday?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/explainer-why-did-huge-swathes-of-the-internet-suddenly-go-offline-yesterday/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/explainer-why-did-huge-swathes-of-the-internet-suddenly-go-offline-yesterday/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:49:59 +0000It caught countless website developers off guard and has left many wondering how protected their cyber systems really are.

When the team behind computer programming language PHP, which powers an estimated 70 per cent of all websites, warned on Wednesday that its software contained “critical vulnerabilities”, it sent the internet into a frenzy.

“Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests,” the developers put it bluntly, but not so simply – “all installations serving web requests” means, in layman’s terms, a website that you can click on.

Users were advised to update immediately or take their sites offline to avoid a cyberattack. While the vulnerability was largely contained within 24 hours of being identified, the fright it has caused will not be easily forgotten.

What is PHP?

“It’s essentially a framework that websites run on,” says Martin Potgieter, the chief technology officer for the South African arm of Integrity 360, a Dublin-based cybersecurity consultancy firm.

Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all

While it’s difficult to say just how many websites run on it, estimates hover around 70 per cent. “A large number of websites on the internet are using it,” Potgieter says.

“It’s an open source code, that’s why it’s so extensively used,” he adds. “Many people might say ‘oh, well, it’s an open source code so that’s why it’s insecure’, but that’s not really the case – it doesn’t make it less secure, just more available.”

And what happened to it on Wednesday?

“A flaw was found in the software that renders the websites using PHP vulnerable to an attack,” Potgieter says. “Once that flaw was discovered, it’s essentially a race between the PHP developers trying to create a patch quicker than news can get out and the details to exploit that vulnerability get out to the world.”

‘Critical vulnerabilities’ found in computer code supporting up to 70% of internet

A “patch” is a corrective measure used to eliminate errors or issues within codes. “It’s very similar to when you get a little notification on your laptop that says Microsoft needs to do updates,” Potgieter goes on. “It’s essentially a change to the code that renders the vulnerability inoperable.”

“Many people were advising to switch off your website, if you can’t patch it, because patching does take time,” he says.

And thus, countless websites suddenly went offline for fear of a cyberattack. You couldn’t read an article from the Journal, you couldn’t buy a screwdriver from Woodie’s DIY and you couldn’t even access the Finnish government’s land registry records.

How serious is this?

“It is quite serious,” Potgieter says.

“If a hacker successfully exploits the vulnerability, they can take control of that system and do what they want with it. That’s obviously high risk – they could take information off of the system or use it for another attack,” he adds.

“There were reports of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities ... I’m not sure if there’s any verified reports that they were successful – but it’s only a matter of time,” he says. If successful, hackers could control website operations or harvest users’ data, among other actions.

More than half of Irish business leaders worried over ‘sophisticated cyber attacks’ by AI

Brian Honan, a cybersecurity expert and chief executive of BH Consulting, says “it’s not rare for a big vulnerability to be found in a piece of software, but I think the impact of this vulnerability will be a surprise due to the fact that the software is used so widely”.

“The vulnerabilities are of a very high severity and would actually enable a potential attacker to remotely control and manage a website to do what they want with it,” he adds.

“The impact of this is huge,” Honan says, “there are websites that are liable to be taken over.”

And who caught the issue?

Honan says “there’s continuous research by security professionals worldwide into looking for weaknesses in software so that they can go back to vendors and recommend to them how to improve the software and make the platforms more secure”.

“With the advent of AI [artificial intelligence] platforms and tools, that makes the research much more scalable and, in some ways, easier to carry out. Researchers can find more vulnerabilities than they could beforehand thanks to AI.”

OpenAI, the force behind ChatGPT, was quick to take credit. “We led a coalition of maintainers, researchers and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP,” the company said in a statement on Tuesday.

“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said.

But Potgieter is less convinced. “Sometimes, these AI labs take credit for AI being used as part of this research, but in many cases, it wouldn’t be possible without humans either starting the process or guiding the AI through it.”

]]>Yong Teck Lim<![CDATA[Mark Duffy’s Axis to ask court to delay ratifying Bawag’s PTSB takeover  ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/mark-duffys-axis-to-ask-court-to-delay-ratifying-bawags-ptsb-takeover/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/mark-duffys-axis-to-ask-court-to-delay-ratifying-bawags-ptsb-takeover/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:23:03 +0000Axis Capital, a corporate advisory firm cofounded by former banker Mark Duffy, said on Thursday it will ask the High Court next week to delay ratifying PTSB’s takeover by Austrian lender Bawag as it seeks to put together an 11th-hour rival bid.

Axis said it will seek an adjournment of up to six weeks of the sanctioning hearing, scheduled for October 27th.

The company said that investment bank Keefe, Bruyette & Woods (KBW) has introduced it to a “large global investment manager”, which is weighing acting as lead investor in the financing of a potential bid.

“The possible funder is evaluating acting as lead anchor investor in the financing of a possible offer, with the balance of the capital to be syndicated to its limited partners and other co-investors,” it said.

KBW has not been engaged by either side. Axis is advised by Berlin-based Quirin Privatbank. Duffy was the chief executive of now-defunct Bank of Scotland (Ireland).

“The possible funder has indicated that completing its confirmatory due diligence is essential before it can syndicate the balance of the capital to its partners and provide a formal letter of support,” Axis said.

]]>Gabby Jones<![CDATA[Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/22/workplace-conflict-costs-millions-annually-but-what-can-be-done-to-remedy-this-problem/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 04:56:00 +0000When I moved here from New York more than three decades ago, I became the default complainer in restaurants. It wasn’t my choice; others expected me to give out for them. I found it strange that even when an Irish friend’s meal was inedible and the service lacking, they’d say everything was okay: “Fine, grand, lovely, thanks.”

If they wanted to express their dissatisfaction with the food, they’d switch plates with me and try to persuade me to gripe on their behalf. Initially, it was amusing, but then it became annoying. Why couldn’t they just complain themselves? Why was this such a big deal to them?

As I only learned after years working and living here – despite being raised abroad by a mother from Carlow and a dad from Dublin – Irish culture is polite and indirect. Avoiding conflict and saving face is a big part of society and often informs how people communicate, or don’t.

Culturally, we know that our strength comes from togetherness and mutual care. Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine: as we live in one another’s shelter. Although we’ve become a more individualistic society in the last 50 years, much of our communalist culture remains in our behaviours and attitudes.

William Corless, a workplace mediator and coach, says cultural norms follow us into the office. When it comes to conflict at work or anywhere, he says, the Irish approach is to avoid it nearly at all costs.

“We’re a land of a thousand welcomes, so we have to be nice,” he says. “But it has to seep out somewhere.” It finds its way into the post-meeting huddle where people are whispering to one another and asking ‘what was that all about?’ instead of complaining constructively. Then it might grow into gossip, then later into a culture of ‘quiet quitting’ or people leaving. In many cases, this can feel more comfortable than addressing an issue head-on.

Both head-on avoidance and conflict itself can be very expensive, professionally and personally, if not well managed. Data indicates that workplace conflict, interpersonal mistreatment and work-related distress result in hundreds of millions of euro in lost productivity annually, plus direct legal awards and reduced performance and efficiency across Irish organisations.

The estimated overall value of lost productivity due to workplace conflict is €239.3 million, with €187.6 million in the private sector and €51.8 million in the public sector, according to the Value of Lost Productivity from Workplace Bullying in Ireland, a 2020 study by NUI Galway’s John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan. Across the entire economy, absenteeism from conflict results in approximately 1.42 million missed days in the private sector and 276,473 days in the public sector annually, says the report.

Employees who reported that they were bullied were considerably more likely to report that they were often or always stressed, while bad and very bad relationships between management and staff were also significantly associated with greater stress, particularly for female employees. That’s according to Bullying and Work-Related Stress in the Irish Workplace, a 2019 study from NUI Galway, by the same researchers plus Michael McDermott and Sharon Walsh.

Remote and hybrid working can also increase the potential for conflict as some of the signals we rely on – body language, physical presence – go missing. Corless likens poor communication and conflict to a screen with missing pixels. We fill in the gaps, but sometimes we fill them in the wrong way and we tend to assume negative intent because we are wired to protect ourselves, he says.

Conflict isn’t always bad and, if well managed, constructive disagreement is the sign of an engaged workforce. High-performing teams aren’t those that never fight – they’re the ones who learn to listen to each other and reset the fastest after disagreements.

When there is an issue, managers carry much of the weight in resolving both indirect and direct conflict. Even so, many find there is little organisational, structural support or training to help them address the problem.

Katie Muldoon, author of Mind Your Self: How Leaders can Integrate AI without Disintegrating Humans, says teams should agree the ground rules together before conflict has a chance to arise.

Start with agreeing on principles, not rules. “A principle is: if we were to do the opposite, would it still be reasonable?” she says. We treat each other kindly is a rule, because nobody would argue for the reverse. Whereas saying we meet in person by default is a principle, because there are good reasons to sometimes do otherwise. When someone wants to break a principle, the team already has a shared reference point for that conversation. Leaders can still make the call, she says, but they should explain it and acknowledge the frustration it may cause.

“You might also ask each individual, ‘what are we here to do as a team?’ You may be surprised to find several different answers, and this may be the original root of conflict in the group.”

Consistency is extremely important for team cohesion too. What unsettles teams is unpredictability, says Muldoon, like “the boss who is warm on Monday and furious on Tuesday”.

She suggests managers think through their communication based on a driving analogy – mirror, signal, manoeuvre. Look in the mirror: what does the team need today? Signal the change in tone. Then manoeuvre and explain why. If, for example, the company’s share price has just dropped, you might be focusing on that when in reality people may be worrying about their jobs and not listening to your plan at all.

Rapport pays off when things get heated. If you know a colleague, Muldoon says, you can tell whether difficult behaviour is a state – a bad day – or a trait. “When we don’t know each other, we avoid conflict. And when it goes underneath the surface, it simmers.” It emerges as missed tasks and skipped meetings. Psychological safety matters here too. “A high-performing team doesn’t make fewer mistakes,” she says. “They learn from them quicker because they can talk about it.”

Managing conflict: Top tips:

1. Put formal structures in place for issues like sexual harassment and bullying;

2. Agree team conflict resolution principles and rules from the start. Formal rules are how we work together. Principles can act as guardrails if disagreement arises. Informal structures like weekly team check-ins, shared learning sessions, and one-to-one meetings set us up for success;

3. Repair before resolving: acknowledge the emotions and manage assumptions first so that tensions can decrease and thinking can re-emerge;

4. Determine if it’s a state or trait. Was the engagement you had with someone indicative of a hard day or a character flaw? Someone may just have been having an awful day, so reflect on your assumptions before reacting;

5. Have the courage to speak up. If team members don’t learn how to disagree constructively, then feelings and resentments get pushed down, and this is where real tension simmers. It’s best to speak up and get it resolved early ... and learn how to complain about your own dinner too.

  • Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

A: The parents have used the small gift exemption here to good effect. This is where anyone can give someone else €3,000 a year, tax-free. That’s a potential gift of €6,000 per calendar year from two parents without reducing a child’s lifetime Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) threshold.

This money has been accumulating in a bare trust for their daughter’s benefit.

Parents considering gifting money in this way should ensure the account is designated as a trust at the outset, says Greg Flanagan, solicitor, and partner at Lavelle Partners.

If it’s simply in a bank account in a parent’s name, Revenue may refuse to recognise it as being in trust for the child, he says. This will have tax implications.

Inheritance tax reform could unlock €170bn sitting on deposit, expert says

The beneficiary of a bare trust is the true owner of the assets, says Catriona Coady, head of tax at Goodbody.

“The trustees merely hold and administer the assets until the beneficiary is legally entitled to take control of them, typically age 18 in the case of a child,” Coady explains.

“Some immediate practical steps these parents can take now are to review the bare trust arrangement, confirm the balance and investment ownership, and plan with their daughter how the account will operate when she turns 18.”

Depending on her needs and wishes, the family could consider a supported bank account, proportionate spending controls agreed with her, a decision-making assistance or co-decision-making agreement, and an enduring power of attorney made by her if she has the required capacity, says Coady.

The reader indicates that in time, her three children will inherit the parents’ estate in equal parts.

Using a discretionary trust may be particularly suitable for this future inheritance, Coady says.

Rather than leaving her a one-third share outright, the parents could revise their will so that her intended share passes to trustees who can apply the assets for her housing, care, education, therapies and wider support, while making controlled payments over time, according to Coady.

These trustees would have full discretion about when and how the daughter receives the money, so it is important that trustees are people who you trust.

Typically, the parents would write a “letter of wishes” to guide the trustees. Although the letter is not legally binding, it is an important guide to the parents’ intentions.

But the existing bare trust fund is different. As the daughter is already the beneficial owner, the parents cannot unilaterally transfer her money into a discretionary trust, Coady says.

“If, once she is 18, she has capacity to make this specific decision, she could choose to settle some or all of the fund into a new trust, but she should receive independent legal advice and understand that she would be giving up an unrestricted entitlement in favour of trustee discretion,” Coady adds.

Her agreement must be voluntary and properly informed. Having a mild learning delay does not of itself mean that someone lacks capacity.

“Capacity is presumed and is assessed in relation to the particular decision, with appropriate support,” Coady says.

All inheritance tax-free thresholds rise in the budget but no wider reforms

“If she lacks capacity to decide whether to place her existing property in a discretionary trust, her parents cannot simply consent on her behalf.”

Advice would be needed on the supported decision-making arrangements available under the assisted decision-making framework.

Any proposal that removes her existing absolute entitlement to the bare trust would require careful scrutiny, Coady says.

‘Payments of trust income may also have income tax implications for the trustees and/or the daughter, depending on how the payment is made and its source’

Catriona Coady, Goodbody

Before any transfer to a discretionary trust is considered, the family should obtain professional advice to determine the legal, tax and social welfare implications of the daughter’s particular circumstances.

However, one of the major benefits of a discretionary trust created under her parents’ will is that for a child with additional needs, their entitlement to State supports such as social welfare, a medical card and disability benefits may be protected. These supports are means-tested.

While assets retained in a discretionary trust are not generally owned by the child, any money or assets paid or appointed to her could become her income or capital and may affect her eligibility for means-tested support.

Get advice before distributions are made, Coady advises.

A discretionary trust is normally subject to tax of 6 per cent of the capital value of the trust fund in year one, and 1 per cent of the capital value for each year afterwards, for as long as the trust continues. If the beneficiary has additional needs and the trust is set up exclusively for them, a discretionary trust tax exemption may apply.

To qualify, Revenue usually requires a medical report or letter from a doctor confirming the child is incapable of managing their own affairs, says Flanagan.

Can I avoid capital gains tax on a rental property by gifting it to my child?

When assets are eventually distributed or appointed out of the trust to a beneficiary, standard gift or inheritance tax rules and thresholds still apply at a rate of 33 per cent on amounts above the child’s €420,000 tax-free threshold, regardless of disability, Flanagan says.

However, depending on the nature and purpose of a payment from the trust, it may be CAT exempt – for example, where funds are used for the beneficiary’s qualifying support and maintenance, or for qualifying expenses related to medical care.

Payments of trust income may also have income tax implications for the trustees and/or the daughter, depending on how the payment is made and its source, so specific tax advice should be taken, Coady says.

The parents might also want to consider the dwelling house exemption – this would allow their daughter to receive the parents’ main home, lived in until the time of their death, tax-free if certain conditions are met, Flanagan says.

If the daughter has occupied this as her main home three years before the date of inheritance, and will continue to do so for at least six years after, and she doesn’t have an interest in another residential property at the date of inheritance or the valuation date – in her own right or in her parents’ will – she could inherit the property tax-free.

An aviation maintenance firm which dismissed one of its co-founders while he was out of work sick following a breakdown in relations at the firm during a €1.2 million pay dispute has been awarded €41,000 at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).

Gerry Burke secured the award against Magellan Aviation Services Ltd on foot of a complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, following the termination of his employment in August 2023 after 33 years at the firm.

Burke was a co-founder and managing director of the company prior to its acquisition in 2013 by the Tokyo-headquartered Marubeni Corporation, the WRC heard.

Having been paid an “eight-figure” sum for his shareholding, Burke moved to Malta for tax reasons, and stepped down as managing director to a new post as director of special projects, the company’s lawyers submitted.

His base salary in that job was €80,000 – later increased to €88,000 – with health insurance, pension contribution and a contractual provision for a €305,000-a-year bonus, bringing his total annual remuneration to €369,786, his lawyers said.

A preliminary objection by the company submitted that the Unfair Dismissals Act did not apply, arguing that Burke lived in Malta, carried out his work “entirely outside” Ireland, and had his salary paid free of Irish income tax. This argument was rejected.

The company received tax advice in 2022 that it was unlawful to pay Burke his salary without deducting either Irish or Maltese tax, it was submitted.

It sought to “regularise” the situation with a new contract increasing Burke’s pay and requiring he pay income tax in Malta, but Burke rejected this, the company submitted further.

Burke said in evidence that the allegations of “tax evasion” levelled at him by the firm were “thrown in to discredit [him] and put a cloud over his reputation”. He was “tax-compliant in Ireland and in Malta”, he said.

His position was that he had contacted Marubeni’s compliance department in 2022 with what his lawyers submitted was a protected disclosure concerning the sale of the company, management practices, and certain pay and contract matters, the tribunal was told.

It was Burke’s case that an investigation into the pay and contract matters proceeded first, with a directive issued from Marubeni that Burke receive a 15 per cent pay rise, which was not actioned, his lawyers submitted further.

The company’s managing director, Niall Duggan, said that when he put the proposal to Burke at a meeting in Zurich, the complainant “suggested that he would move to Dubai”.

Duggan added that Burke “intended to sue [the company] if it took action to ensure that it complied with [Malta’s] tax legislation”.

Burke agreed he had threatened an injunction but said that without the firm sharing its tax advice with him, he could not reasonably agree to the company’s plans to establish a company in Malta and make him an employee there.

In 2023, Duggan said, “matters became increasingly fractious”, with Burke initiating a High Court action in Ireland and seeking to escalate the dispute to the leadership of the Marubeni Corporation in Japan.

In March that year, Burke underwent “serious surgery”, his legal team submitted. The actions of Magellan caused him “stress and strain” and delayed his recovery, it was further submitted.

After about five months’ absence due to sick leave, the company terminated Burke’s employment on the basis of disability, the tribunal noted.

There was “an express contractual provision under which an executive is automatically deemed to have a disability following an extended absence from work due to ill-health” in Burke’s employment contract, the adjudication officer noted.

Although Burke sought reinstatement as his preferred remedy for the dismissal, his legal papers calculated his total losses at more than €1.2 million, the WRC recorded.

The WRC noted that Burke had alleged non-payment of salary going back to 2020, and had initiated separate proceedings in the High Court.

Ruling the dismissal unfair, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska wrote: “I cannot accept that other matters, some of them still remaining unresolved, had no impact on the respondent’s decision to dismiss [Burke], Sobanska wrote.

She was not satisfied the termination arose “wholly or mainly” due to any question of Burke’s capability, she wrote.

However, she found she could not order reinstatement on the basis of “fractious relationships” and “tension between the parties”.

Sobanska wrote that €41,434.08, about six months’ base salary, was a “just and equitable” award for the dismissal.

This was because she could not take Burke’s claimed bonus payments into account, and she regarded his efforts to seek new work to be “inadequate”.

Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors. Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley.

Meet the Americans moving to Ireland for a better life

Securing a job offer is the first step, as employers often assess visa requirements early in the hiring process, according to Breda Dooley, head of recruitment at Matrix.

Where permits are required, timelines and recruitment decisions can be impacted, she says.

The role must have a minimum salary of €36,605, though the salary for meat processors, horticultural workers, healthcare assistants and home carers must be at least €32,691.

]]>Jim Vondruska<![CDATA[Are women in your workplace earning less? A new Government website will make it easier for you to find out.

Ireland’s national gender pay gap stands at 8.3 per cent, according to figures quoted by the Department of Equality this year. That’s the average difference in pay between all men and all women in the workforce. If you’re a woman working in an organisation on the wrong side of the gap, it pays to know about it.

New data published from next month aims to lift the lid on gaps in pay and equip you to find out how your workplace measures up.

New portal

By the end of November, all employers with more than 50 employees must publish data about their gender pay gap to a new public gender pay gap portal.

The gender pay gap is the average difference in pay between all men and all women in an organisation. If you are a woman working in an organisation where there is a big gap, it doesn’t bode well for your finances.

The pay portal has been open for voluntary reporting since last year and viewable to the public since June, but publication by employers is about to become mandatory.

The Employment Equality Bill 2026 will be enacted in the coming weeks, with individual company gender pay gap figures for 2026 available to view by the end of November, Minister for Equality Norma Foley told the Dáil last week.

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) put Ireland’s national gender pay gap at 9.6 per cent in 2022. Mean hourly earnings for men were €27.73 and €25.06 for women, a gap of €2.67.

As age increases, the gender pay gap grows. The biggest gap was in the 50-59 age group at 16.7 per cent, with men earning €33.03 and women earning €27.51.

Sectors such as construction, aviation and finance tend to show wider gaps due to male-dominated senior roles, while education and healthcare often show the opposite trend.

In many cases, it’s less about pay rates and more about representation at senior levels, says UCD’s Professional Academy.

It’s important to note the gender pay gap is not a test of whether men and women in an organisation are paid equally for the same work – that’s already required by law. Rather, it highlights imbalances that influence how opportunities are distributed, according to the academy.

If your organisation has a big gender pay gap, there may be some telltale signs.

There are probably fewer women in senior or higher-paid roles; there is an over-representation of women in lower-paid or part-time roles in a company; maybe there is unconscious bias or barriers to the progression of women; there is a culture where availing of hybrid working is frowned on; or maybe there is a culture where the men who work there never take leave for caring responsibilities.

Female participation in Irish workforce jumps 90% since 2000

Some or all of these characteristics can contribute to a workplace where pay between genders is out of whack.

If you work in or are interviewing for a role in an organisation with a big pay gap, the impact can ripple far beyond your pay cheque.

Lower average pay than male colleagues in an organisation can mean women there get a smaller percentage pay rise than male colleagues, receive a less generous pay-linked bonus, are unable to borrow as much their male colleagues can to buy a house, and end up with smaller pensions in retirement.

If you are already in a job or scouting for a new one, the new pay gap portal will make it easier to look under the bonnet and see the reality of the hiring, pay, promotion practices and culture there.

Scores on the doors

Gender pay gap reporting requires employers to choose a snapshot day in June this year, and use pay information for the previous 12 months for their pay gap calculations. Employers then have five months to publish their report, by the end of November.

Some 1,000 employers have now created accounts on the portal in preparation for publishing their reports by the end of next month, the Department of Equality says.

Some firms have been proactive, voluntarily publishing their 2025 pay gap data to the portal. You’ll find 410 such reports already published.

Searching the portal by company name and looking for the mean, or average gender pay gap, is a useful metric for employees, says Michelle McDonagh, chief client officer at human resource management consultancy Adare.

If you see a large gender pay gap percentage, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the organisation is paying women unfairly, says McDonagh.

“Gender pay gap measures the pay of all men and compares it against all women. There is no allowance for the type of role, length of service, level of seniority or expertise,” she says.

“It’s a blunt instrument in that regard.”

The gender pay gap figure, however, is a useful indicator of hiring and promotion practices, policies and culture in a company.

Being a working mother is a horror show at times. The stress can be crippling

A zero per cent pay gap is the ideal. That would mean men and women’s pay is perfectly balanced.

A positive gender pay gap, of five per cent for example, means women earn five per cent less on average than men. A negative, or minus gap, means men earn less than women on average.

“Most organisations will have a positive figure because in most organisations, women will earn less than men on average,” says McDonagh.

Comparing companies by sector can provide an interesting perspective.

Take the telecommunications, computer programming and consulting sector in the data, for example. This is one of the most highly remunerated sectors in the country. Consultancy firm Deloitte has been proactive in publishing its data and reports a 5.2 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in favour of men.

Another useful search in the portal is “distribution of gender by pay quartile”. This requires bosses to segment their workforce by pay band and tell you the balance of men and women in each of four different bands. Looking at Deloitte, there were 10 per cent more women than men in the lower middle pay band in 2025, but 4 per cent more men than women in the very top pay band.

“One of the trends we tend to see in companies is if there are a lot of females coming into lower-paid roles and for whatever reason they are not progressing through the ranks,” says McDonagh.

“Then you see a lot of males in the higher-paid roles and women’s representation drops away as they move through those different pay quartiles.”

What top CEO pay and gender pay gap reporting tell us about Irish business

Companies are required to publish a statement about what is causing their pay gap and what they are going to do about it.

Deloitte’s statement says the company has met its target of 35 per cent female partners by 2025.

“We aim to increase this to 40 per cent by 2027, with a 50 per cent longer-term goal,” according to the firm.

Data for PwC shows a 1.6 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in the mean hourly pay of female and male employees.

Women and men are 50:50 in the lowest pay quartile, but there are 10 per cent more women than men in the topmost pay quartile.

‘Women make up at least half of our population. This, in turn, has had a significant influence on the outcome of our gender pay gap analysis,” says PwC.

KPMG, Ernst & Young (EY) or Accenture have not published data on the portal for 2025. They will be required to publish their 2026 data by the end of November.

They were required to publish 2025 pay gap data on their own websites, however.

KPMG reports an average gender pay gap of 11.1 per cent for 2025 – the organisation comprises 51 per cent women and 49 per cent men. There are more women than men in all three lower pay quartiles, but 11 per cent more men at the top pay quartile.

There is a 23.2 per cent average bonus gap between men and women at the consulting firm, its report says.

At partner level, women represent 24 per cent of partners. The pay gap between female and male partners is 5.6 per cent.

Pay transparency rules could cause conflict in workplaces, say HR and law experts

The mean pay gap at Accenture for 2025 is 9.2 per cent. The number of women and men are almost equal in all pay quartiles – except at the top one where there are 10 per cent more men in the highest pay grade.

The mean pay gap at EY for 2025 is 6.5 per cent. Some 71 per cent of partners are male.

Meta Platforms Ireland, which employs 95 per cent of Meta’s staff here, has a 2025 gender pay gap of 26.5 per cent, and an average bonus pay gap of 37 per cent.

The company employs an almost equal number of men and women. The number of women at Meta is greatest in its lowest pay quartile, where there are 62 per cent women, and the number of women is fewest in the highest pay quartile, where there are 63 per cent men.

Women are better represented in non-tech roles in the company, Meta says. Tech roles, like software engineers, are typically paid more in the market, and this has a disproportionate impact on pay gaps, it says.

The bonus gap is higher than the hourly pay gap, which is primarily driven by higher tech equity, it says.

Hooke & MacDonald is the only large real estate firm to have voluntarily published its gender pay gap data to the Government portal for 2025. It reports a 13 per cent gender pay gap in the mean hourly pay of female employees and of male employees.

“We are clear that our pay gap arises as a result of a greater proportion of males in senior positions in specific areas of the business and on higher pay points within those grades – due to longer service in those roles. This significantly contributes to the pay gap,” the company says.

Government organisations have been busy reporting their data too.

An Coimiusiún Pleanála, for example, had a 6.1 per cent gender pay gap in 2025. It’s an improvement of 9.4 per cent on the previous year.

This is down to a relatively higher share of roles taken up by women in administrative grades, which have a lower average hourly pay than other grades, it says.

There are 8 per cent more women than men in the second-from-top pay band, but 12 per cent more men in the top band.

“A great deal of effort [is being made] in recent years to improve our gender balance at senior manager level, including actively supporting family-friendly initiatives such as hybrid working, work sharing, statutory leave schemes and the shorter working year scheme,” says the commission.

The commission reported its 2025 pay gap in three categories – men, women and non-binary – but says the format of the portal makes it impossible to fully report on pay gap statistics for the three groups.

An Post reports a zero gender pay gap for the fifth consecutive year. Its 2025 data shows a mean hourly gender pay gap of minus 4.85 per cent in favour of women. It has an equal percentage of male and female executive directors.

Banking and finance sectors slow to disclose salary information, data shows

Perception

Gender pay gap stats may be particularly beneficial to women in the middle pay quartile, says McDonagh.

“If you can see the norm in your company is for more male representation at the top, maybe you hadn’t realised that’s the context you are working in – the report will tell you that,” says McDonagh.

“Then you are going to have to take charge of your own career, you are going to have to drive it yourself.

“If the stats tell you that men in your organisation have the majority of the income, you are going to have to drive those conversations with your manager yourself to make sure you are getting the opportunity to progress. Keep asking the question, what do I have to do to move up?”

The data is a very public opening of the kimono for organisations, and at a time when HR headcount and diversity and inclusion initiatives are under fire.

“Some 64 per cent of employers have identified employee perception as their biggest concern about publication of their gender pay gap report,” says Adare’s McDonagh of her company’s most recent HR Barometer data.

While gender pay gap statistics can be a bit of a blunt instrument, the statement employers are required to publish explaining the data can be insightful, says McDonagh.

This self-examination requires them to explain the cause of their gender pay gap and what they are going to do about it.

Work to transpose the remaining parts of the European Union (EU) Pay Transparency Directive is continuing, the department says. This will include the obligation for employers to carry out a gender-neutral job evaluation. This requires employers to examine why they are remunerating some types of work more than others. It involves assessing the value of different types of work in their organisation, putting work of similar value into the same category and ensuring these people are similarly paid.

This means equal pay for those doing work of the same value too – even if that work looks quite different.

In UK clothing retailer Next, for example, the mostly female sales staff were found to be earning less than the company’s mostly male warehouse workers. Even though their jobs seem different, the retail staff contributed work of equal value to the warehouse workers, a tribunal found.

Employers will be invited to training to help them compare work objectively – based on skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions – to eliminate gender pay gaps and bias.

Done right, this could upend old pay structures that have unfairly rewarded some skills over others, for no objective reason.

]]><![CDATA[Why developers are turning to hotels, not apartments]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/why-developers-are-turning-to-hotels-not-apartments/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/21/why-developers-are-turning-to-hotels-not-apartments/Wed, 21 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The cracks are starting to show. After years of defying reality about the Dublin office market’s prospects, developers are now embracing the hotel market as never before.

The latest convert is the German property group KGAL, which wants to knock down an office block on Dublin’s Golden Lane and build a 225-bedroom hotel. They follow in the footsteps of Core Capital’s Derek McGrath and of Johnny Ronan’s eponymous property group, both of which have reversed planned office developments.

The change of heart reflects an anaemic market for office space in Dublin, with CBRE expecting the take-up of office space this year to be roughly in line with last year but below the long-run average. They see a few bright spots on the horizon and tentative signs of the new development cycle, helped somewhat counter-intuitively by demand from artificial intelligence companies.

A more downbeat view is expressed by Peter Keegan, the director of debt and structured finance at CBRE, in a letter submitted to Dublin City Council as part of the KGAL planning application. It can be paraphrased as saying that, notwithstanding the green shoots mentioned above, lenders are wary of office development in Dublin.

Or, as Keegan put it, “there will be much deeper liquidity from debt providers for the development of a hotel on the site versus a new office building ... this is a development which will be received more positively as a hotel project than a speculative office scheme”.

Lenders call the shots in property development, and their enthusiasm for hotel projects is easy to understand. There is a well-documented shortage of hotel rooms in the capital, as evidenced by high occupancy rates. The shortfall is put at 3,600 beds, which equates to 20 or so hotels along the lines of the one planned by KGAL.

The downside with hotels is you have to find someone to run it for you, but if you can get more than 80 per cent occupancy, you will do well. It’s not a one-way bet. About 2,600 new beds are already in the pipeline, according to consultants Mitchell McDermott. The window of opportunity is closing and hence the stampede towards hoteliership by office developers.

From this perspective, their lack of enthusiasm for building apartments is hard to understand given the much larger and open-ended demand – 50,000 homes a year for the foreseeable future.

Again, the KGAL planning application is instructive. It contains an assessment of the site’s potential for an apartment development. The planning report argues that if the various rules and regulations pertaining to apartments – such as access to daylight and minimum open spaces – were to be complied with, then the maximum number of apartments that could be built on the site is between 50 and 60 units. This would not be “viable” even though it is a 10-minute walk from Grafton Street.

The site’s suitability for student accommodation is also deemed not to be “viable”. Urbanest, the student accommodation provider, kindly supplied a letter saying planning constraints “render it not possible” for student accommodation of sufficient scale to be viable. Two-hundred bed spaces would be needed.

Viability gets mentioned a lot in the KGAL planning application, but it is not really defined. Presumably what they are talking about is commercial viability and that is something of movable feast.

It takes a lot of factors into account, including the value of the site for other uses, the costs of construction and the availability and cost of debt financing. It also includes opportunity cost – whether you might make more money using the debt and resources required for Golden Lane elsewhere.

Viability is thus not the same thing as profitability. It may well be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane, but just not as profitable as building a hotel.

Whether it is “viable” to choose an option that delivers a lower profit is another question entirely. It is perfectly reasonable for KGAL to argue it is not viable for them to choose an option – such as apartments instead of a hotel – that will deliver a lower return to their investors.

But that does not mean it would not be viable for someone else with access to cheaper funding and different objectives, such as the Land Development Agency, to build apartments.

Dublin city planners would be doing us some service if they looked a little deeper into the question of viability. Is KGAL saying it would not be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane or simply that it would be more profitable to build a hotel?

The planners might then apply their own definition of viability. It would seem axiomatic that if a 60-unit apartment development could be built at a profit, it would be more than viable from the perspective of the Government’s obligation to house people.

The State planning authority said the plans “would constitute overdevelopment” and “would seriously injure the residential and visual amenities of property in the vicinity of the site”.

In supporting documents submitted last week to the council, a town planning consultancy firm working on behalf of Kelland Homes said that the “revised proposals” are “substantially different” from the original development and its volume has been “significantly reduced”.

The developer is now seeking permission to construct 10 town houses of three or four bedrooms and 10 apartments of two or three bedrooms, not exceeding three storeys in height, the renewed planning application reads.

The site currently hosts two semidetached bungalows, which Kelland Homes proposes to partially demolish and later refurbish. The two properties sit on a combined 0.43 hectares, according to data from Tailte Éireann, which maintains the State’s official land register.

One of the homes, 21 Monaloe Cottages, was sold in October 2020 for €1,625,000, while the adjoining 20 Monaloe Cottages property was sold in April 2026 for €900,000, according to the Property Price Register. Both cottages had two bedrooms at the time of their sale.

Kelland Homes also proposes “the relocation of the existing bus shelter and associated bus stop on Clonkeen Road”, which services the Dublin Bus L26 route to Blackrock Dart station, to provide space for the development’s entrance.

]]>Frank_U

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445841/">
   <title>Bisher keine Angriffe in Österreich bekannt</title>
   <description>Weltweit hat es Millionen Versuche von Cyberangriffen auf Websites gegeben, nachdem am Mittwoch gravierende Sicherheitslücken in der Programmiersprache PHP bekanntgeworden waren. Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year.

The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself.

Warto przypomnieć:
▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości.
▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv

— Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026

Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons.

After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused.

On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then.

Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week.

"Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026

On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway.

The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban.

Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition.

 

Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN.

The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”.

Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty.

A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”.

However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026

The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”.

In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations.

Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia.

Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states.
