The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies.

Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades.

During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”.

📍 New Delhi | Premier @donaldtusk spotkał się z Premierem Indii @narendramodi. pic.twitter.com/Y9HPLQsvf4

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 22, 2026

Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies.

Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20.

“The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said.

Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.”

 

Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market.

Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”.

“Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.”

However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals.

The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible".

"Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility.

To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations.

Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people.

The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors.

Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS).

Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026

The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations.

Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War.

“In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”.

The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.

]]> How will recent scandals affect Polish politics? https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/22/how-will-recent-scandals-affect-polish-politics/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 09:56:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105869 Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals now rarely have the dramatic impact they once did.]]>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis.

Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.

He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”.

The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała.

However, Poland has a strict policy of not allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in tournaments on its territory. This year, it banned them from taking part in a World Cup ski jumping event. It was also removed as host of two European junior weightlifting championships for banning Russian and Belarusian athletes.

Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams.

Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty.

— Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026

The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation.

The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures.

Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies.

 

“The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.”

The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation.

Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland.

Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia.

Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU.

This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace.

What appears to be a drone exploded…

— Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026

On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object.

President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”.

Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace.

“I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT.

 

However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”.

Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country.

In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”.

Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”.

We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia.

We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have…

— Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026

Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian.

“We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.”

The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was.

Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming.

On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself.

It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Thu, 22 Oct 2026 18:12:42 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Braddick sets out her vision for banking watchdog with £2bn overhaul https://www.cityam.com/braddick-sets-out-her-vision-for-banking-watchdog-with-2bn-overhaul/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 20:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2468359

Katharine Braddick has kicked off her revamp of the UK banking’s watchdog with a regulatory overhaul aiming to generate £2bn in savings for City firms. The Prudential Regulation Authority chief, who took the reins in July, told a City audience on Thursday evening the watchdog would focus on four key priorities of resilience, growth, innovation [...]]]>

Katharine Braddick has kicked off her revamp of the UK banking’s watchdog with a regulatory overhaul aiming to generate £2bn in savings for City firms.

The Prudential Regulation Authority chief, who took the reins in July, told a City audience on Thursday evening the watchdog would focus on four key priorities of resilience, growth, innovation and transparency over the next 10 years. 

“Our task is to determine what the PRA must deliver in its second decade and how to create the regulator the UK will need for the future,” Braddick said.

The remarks came as Braddick – in tandem with the Financial Conduct Authority – unveiled an overhaul of the Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SM&CR) with a package estimated to save financial firms £2bn over 10 years.

Reforms included scrapping the Certification regime, which removes the requirement to annually assess, certify and publicly register around 139,000 non-senior management staff. 

Pre-approvals for non-executive senior roles will also be replaced by a simple notification process to the FCA, while mandatory pre-approvals will be maintained strictly for core executive leaders. 

“Achieving sustained and sustainable growth is the key economic policy question of this moment and regulation has its part to play, even if it is rarely the determinative factor,” Braddick said during her Mansion House address.

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves appointed Bradick to the post after former boss Sam Woods’ term finished.

Braddick was viewed as the “outsider” candidate, joining the regulator after a four-year stint as head of strategic policy at Barclays. She is understood to have beaten Bank of England incumbent David Bailey to the position.

Banking watchdog to ramp up cyber focus as threats grow 

Braddick said the PRA would develop its secondary growth objective to consider how the regulator’s work “influences the investment environment, the availability of capital for the firms we regulate and the pricing of the services they provide”.

“This framework will help ensure our regime remains relevant, effective, and proportionate,” she said.

Regulators will also raise the financial thresholds for consumer credit lenders and asset managers by nearly 50 per cent, meaning enhanced SM&CR requirements will fall on the largest institutions.

Braddick also announced the creation of a new unit sitting inside the PRA that will act as a “centre of excellence for operational and cyber resilience”.

Industry figures have sounded the alarm over the growing threat posed by new technology in the last year. Former HSBC UK chief Ian Stuart last year said the risk of cyber-attacks “keeps [him] awake at night” and the firm was being “attacked all the time”.

The Treasury Select Committee took aim at regulators this year for “not doing enough to manage the risks presented by AI”.

Braddick said: “The PRA is a world-class regulator. To continue to be so, we must become a world leading technologically enabled regulator.” 

She added the cyber challenge was an area where the PRA “can and do partner effectively with industry and our international counterparts to progress our understanding of both risks and mitigants”.

The unchecked rise of artificial intelligence means the level of risk facing the financial system is currently “on steroids”, according to the boss of the Financial Conduct Authority, who warned that excessive “tick-box” rulemaking would fail to keep pace with increasingly complex threats.

Prima Facie review and star rating: ★★★★

In London, only 3 per cent of reported rapes lead to a suspect being charged. It is a fact so shocking that even people with no interest in the courts recite it. It is the problem that forms the backdrop of Suzie Miller’s very good 2022 play of the same name as this film, which starred Killing Eve actor Jodie Comer, who in a 100 minutes of theatre astonishingly played every character from the court judge to the victim. 

Miller’s writing, for which she won the Olivier Award in 2023, extracts a compelling human story out of this institutional crisis. Prima Facie follows Tessa Ensler, a successful criminal defence barrister who has become rich protecting men who are probably guilty of crimes by finding legal loopholes. But an incident in her personal life forces her to rethink the morality of her work. 

Prima Facie: film can be didactic

Wicked’s Cynthia Erivo takes over from Comer for Susanna White’s screen adaptation, alongside a supporting cast (Erivo played dozens of characters was presumably harder to land on film). Still, a similar sense of horror is conjured. As Ensler, Erivo brings the sort of muscular fortitude that demonstrates how this young working class woman would graduate to this kind of job that’s typically reserved for the private schooled elite. She is also brilliant at conveying Ensler’s vulnerability; as she experiences a personal breakdown, Erivo’s angular, cocksure barrister softens, her eyes becoming wide chasms of overwhelm.

There’s an attempt to retain the character-driven intensity of the stage production, via a wealth of tracking shots of Erivo walking past London courthouses and along the river while the camera lingers close. It’s straightforwardly shot and rarely distracted by bells and whistles.

Harrowing plot

There have been complaints of didacticness, and at a few points, I am taken briefly out of the action when a line or two is too on-the-nose, moralising about the ways the legal system needs to change. But I’d argue that some of this is inevitable. The story is set in a courtroom, the literal bedrock for conversations about ways to change the world. The one place where you do get to stand up and have your say. Perhaps Prima Facie has an excuse to tell us how to feel more than most. 

It’s certainly a minor distraction from a terrific depiction of the injustices so many women face, and a truly harrowing plot – multiple women ran out in tears during the London Film Festival screening, and this male critic joined them in weeping throughout. Like the West End show, this Prima Facie finds a compelling and totally shocking human story amid a legal system that seems to have forgotten about the victims. 

Prima Facie is in UK cinemas on 13 November 2026

Investing in a football stadium can be the difference between sinking and swimming and the government must play a role, writes Joseph Smith.

It is fair to say that the Independent Football Regulator’s draft State of the Game report provides the most comprehensive analysis of English football’s finances to date. Published last week and open for consultation until the end of the year, it highlights that while English football is both highly competitive and wealthy it faces significant financial risk.

The report’s key findings? That 94 per cent of clubs in the top five divisions – from the Premier League down to the National League – operated at a loss, and that two thirds could not survive 90 days without additional funding from existing owners. Nearly 20 EFL and National League clubs reported non-player operating cost figures that were higher than their total revenues.

The regulator was established because parliament determined that football clubs are not ordinary businesses. Since a club cannot be easily replaced if it fails, the Football Governance Act imposes a level of scrutiny uncommon in most industries.

The long-standing debate

Debate has long focused on television revenue – which for the Premier League is into the billions – including redistribution and parachute payments from the top flight. However, the regulator highlights that matchday income becomes increasingly important further down the league pyramid. In the top division it represented 14 per cent of revenue but that rises to 19 per cent in the Championship and 35 per cent in Leagues One and Two.

Matchday income is therefore essential, and stadium improvements can be a direct way to achieve this. Larger stadiums allow for more ticket sales where demand exists, and enhanced facilities support higher-value matchday and commercial activities – tiers of premium seating have been a popular addition to many stadiums over the last decade. The regulator concludes that investment in stadiums and infrastructure has significantly increased revenue for the largest clubs.

Premier League clubs benefit from higher ticket prices, stronger demand and corporate hospitality, and invested £2.2bn in infrastructure between 2021/22 and 2024/25. By contrast, League Two clubs invested only £16m. Large clubs can also manage delays and rising costs, while smaller clubs have limited capacity to do so.

Stadium investment key

Luton Town is an example of this; the club announced plans to move from Kenilworth Road to Power Court in 2016 but since then the club has moved between divisions while the stadium project faced planning, legal and design hurdles. For smaller clubs such delays could be the difference between spades in the ground and nothing at all.

The government must therefore step up and reduce some of the planning, transport, land and infrastructure barriers that hinder private investment. The Stadium Regeneration Accelerator announced earlier this year will offer a clear incentive to focus on the largest projects. But the true measure of the initiative is whether government involvement enables projects to go ahead that otherwise would not.

Stadium investment is part of the solution to a problem that plagues most of the sport. The government should continue supporting major regeneration schemes that create housing, jobs and investment, but the opportunity extends further. The true value of the Stadium Regeneration Accelerator lies in helping viable projects lower down the pyramid overcome barriers that clubs cannot address alone. This would not only support regeneration around football grounds but also help vulnerable clubs build stronger businesses.

Joseph Smith is a senior consultant at Henham Strategy

Lawyers have been warned they remain accountable for supervising AI use within their law firm, particularly when junior employees are operating the technology.

The Law Society, an independent body that represents solicitors in England and Wales, issued new guidance on Wednesday setting out the appropriate use of AI in legal work, meaning lawyers cannot blame the technology – or junior employees – for any mistakes it makes.

The guidance states that lawyers’ “professional duties and obligations apply in the same way whether AI or other technologies were used” by the solicitor themselves “or by anyone under that solicitor’s supervision to assist with that work.”

Vice-Chair of the City of London Law Society’s AI Committee Kerry Westland, told City AM that while AI “has significant potential to support lawyers at every level” it “does not displace firms’ existing duties of competence, supervision and accountability.”

“Firms will need to ensure that junior lawyers are trained to use AI critically and safely, while continuing to develop the legal judgement and practical skills that come from properly supervised experience. The Committee will consider the guidance as part of its ongoing work on the impact of AI across CLLS member firms,” Westland said.

The Law Society added that AI is “no substitute for junior lawyers” and those which are responsible for junior colleagues must make sure the tech does not “replace opportunities”, including how to “identify errors, omissions and unsupported propositions.”

“Solicitors and law firms should choose their AI tools carefully and always check that legal work meets their professional standards. Over-reliance on AI systems may result in a catastrophic gap of future legal skills and knowledge,” Brett Dixon, president of the Law Society, said.

The legal watchdog, the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), issued a similar warning in August noting that lawyers who supervise junior colleagues “may also be found to have breached regulatory requirements and professional duties if false citations are put before the court without adequate review and/or supervision.”

Legal sectors’ AI use under the microscope

This comes as lawyers and law firms across London and the rest of the UK are being closely watched by the courts and legal regulators and reprimanded for any mistakes made in AI-assisted legal work.

Top City firm Pinsent Masons was slammed by a High Court judge in May for sending misleading letters to the court containing false legal information. The firm admitted that an AI tool had been used by the junior solicitor to research the legal issue, and to later draft the second letter.

In September, an immigration lawyer, Abhisek Kumar, who was referred to a Tribunal after a criminal conviction became the first solicitor in the UK to be struck off after using AI-generated evidence as part of his own defence.

The Upper Tribunal issued a warning earlier this year in an immigration case on the serious risks of using AI in court documents, including in legal professional privilege.

The lawyers had either used AI themselves or instructed their junior staff to use it to draft an immigration judicial review application which contained inaccurate citations of case law.

The Tribunal reminded lawyers that “a supervisor who fails to ensure that the work of a more junior fee-earner does not contain false cases or citations is likely to be more culpable than a lawyer who fails to ensure that his own work is free from such ‘hallucinations’.”

Lidl and Aldi are currently excluded from a law which bans the UK’s biggest supermarket chains from engaging in so-called ‘landblocking‘. Top grocers have already warned that the existing rules allowed the two German discounters to use a “problematic” loophole to block rivals from opening nearby.

However, the competition regulator is now set to force the two grocers to comply. 

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) on Thursday confirmed its provisional decision to extend the Controlled Land Order to cover Aldi and Lidl. 

The pair had previously been excluded from the rules because they were classed as “limited assortment discounters”. But the CMA has said it will now categorise the two firms as “large grocery retailers” because of their rapid expansion in recent years. 

Lidl and Aldi will join Asda, Co-op, Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose in being blocked from using these land laws to gain an advantage over their rivals. 

Budget supermarket Iceland, which is not covered by the land order, welcomed the CMA’s provisional decision.

In a letter to the regulator, published on Thursday, the company said existing rules allowed Aldi and Lidl to “deploy problematic land arrangements […] at scale and in a way that could have a material adverse impact on competition for groceries across the UK market”. 

Though the two German discounters occupied a relatively small part of the UK’s grocery market when the Controlled Land Order was set up, the firms “now each exert a significant and compelling degree of competitive influence in the UK grocery market,” Iceland said.

Lidl and Aldi ‘shielded from competition’

Grocers Morrisons, Waitrose and Iceland each wrote to the CMA, expressing concerns that Lidl and Aldi are preparing to expand further in the UK, citing plans to reach 1,500 stores each.

Aldi and Lidl have previously claimed they should not be classed as large grocery retailers because they offer fewer products than their rivals. 

But Morrisons told the CMA that both supermarket chains “publicly market their product range as being suitable for a full weekly shop” and pose “intense competition” even in the categories they claim to be weak in.

A Waitrose spokesperson wrote to the regulator, warning that it had seen “first hand” Lidl’s use of the land order to “restrict the ability of other grocery retailers to open new stores and shield Lidl from local competition”.

The up-market grocer said the CMA should impose its rulings as soon as possible. “It is important that these decisions are taken without further delay to ensure there is equal opportunity in the competition between LGRs and Aldi and Lidl to secure further sites for grocery retail.”

Juliette Enser, executive director for competition enforcement at the regulator, said the new rules will “help level the playing field and make sure shoppers get the best choice of products and prices in their area”.

Responding to the CMA’s provisional ruling in August, Lidl and Aldi said the crackdown would not slow their plans to expand rapidly in the UK. 

Commenting on the decision, an Aldi spokesperson said: “We remain firmly committed to opening hundreds of new stores across the country, bringing Aldi’s unbeatable value and award-winning quality to even more customers.

A Lidl spokesperson said: “As a discounter, we have always welcomed and embraced competition within the market, and our focus remains on continuing to open new stores and bringing our high-quality, lowest-priced groceries to even more communities.”

Lewisham’s £1.5bn shopping centre redevelopment freeze, caused by a breakdown between Landsec and the Council, has left residents, traders, and the town centre stranded in uncertainty, says Sergiy Lesyk

Lewisham shows how a council can lose a £1.5bn scheme and gain nothing.

Landsec, the property company that has owned Lewisham Shopping Centre for more than 20 years, has put its £1.5bn redevelopment of the centre on hold. Councillors approved the scheme in October 2025, and work had been due to start in 2027. Now nobody can say when, or whether, anything will happen.

You don’t have to have liked the plans to see the problem that residents and traders in Lewisham now face.

Landsec gave two reasons: one was the cost of building in London, the other was the Council. In Landsec’s words, recent statements from the Council “make clear that the administration is not able to support the next phase of land assembly needed to unlock delivery without a significant increase in affordable housing.”

On a social video, the mayor, Liam Shrivastava, had the temerity to state “the conditions for such developments are simply not favourable right now”, and that “the way out of the housing crisis is through building social housing.”

The mayor was elected on a promise of 1,000 new social rent homes. Instead, the plan to replace the shopping centre with 1,744 homes, including 98 for social rent and 231 at discounted rents or for key workers, will no longer be built. The shopping centre development took about five years to approve, so who really thinks this council will match it any time soon?

Boots has left its high street unit, which sits in the first phase, for a unit inside the centre. Marks & Spencer, a fixture in Lewisham for almost a century, has closed for good, Natwest has said it will close its branch, and the Model Market food hall still hasn’t reopened.

Landsec itself says the 1970s building is no longer fit for purpose, as it had been expected to be demolished. 

Labour, which approved the scheme, and the Greens, who now run the Council, are busy blaming each other, and the mayor is blaming the government. Finger-pointing won’t build a single home or fill a single empty unit.

Lewisham is being let down

And the drift goes well beyond the shopping centre. A short walk away, the 649 homes of the Filigree at Lewisham Gateway have stood empty since a flood in February 2025, and residents won’t be back before October 2027. Nearby, one resident told us that food waste bins turned up at their block with no guidance and no collections. The building manager has had to tell everyone not to use them until the council explains what happens next. Even the council’s own website can’t seem to agree on whether flats are getting food waste collections.

This matters well beyond SE13. London needs homes, and it needs investors with the long-term support and confidence of local councils to build them. 

So what should happen now?

First, the council should be straight with residents about what it told Landsec and what it now expects to happen to the site.

Second, it should publish a support plan for the traders caught up in the uncertainty, because they’re paying for decisions they didn’t make.

Third, and most importantly, it should set out its own plan for Lewisham town centre. If this scheme wasn’t good enough, the Council needs to show what would be, who will build it, and when.

Lewisham Conservatives support homes and investment in Lewisham, but not a town centre left in limbo. Residents were promised new homes, a new town centre and a new community. They’ve been let down. The council can’t build any of it until it first rebuilds their trust.

Sergiy Lesyk is chairman of Lewisham Conservatives

Could a day spent learning to tell your Pinots from your plonks at London’s WSET turn the average wine-lover into a bona fide wine connoisseur? Carys Sharkey finds out

The UK’s wine sector is going through a period of chop and change. The UK is still the second largest importer of wine in the world, behind only the US (and behind Germany if based on volume rather than value, respect). But as boiling temperatures stretch grape harvests to the brink in much of Europe, the UK’s domestic growing market is ripening. As grape production becomes more rooted in our landscape, will wine consumption in turn shake up our lager-drenched culture? 

A recent study by the Wine and Spirit Trade Association (WSTA) has found that although wine consumption is slowing, there is a trend towards premiumisation. In other words, less plonk more Planque. The average Brit drinks 17.5 bottles of wine a year, which to me feels puritanically low. This summer, my GP gave me a gentle scolding over my own wine consumption (which was concerning because I was lying).

But I love wine even if I’ve never been on totally sure footing talking about it. In an attempt to rationalise what I was pounding down over lockdown, I read the excellent ‘Wine from Another Galaxy’ by the Noble Rot boys. I occasionally read wine columns, a little wonkish on the vine, and diligently take pictures of bottles I drink in restaurants for the pseudo camera roll archive. Remembering wine when you don’t really know wine and are drinking said wine is a challenge in itself. But earlier this year I decided it was time to get a proper schooling in how to talk about – or at least convince others I can talk about – wine.

Bermondsey Street is one of the most European feeling streets in London. Bustling with bars and cafes, The White Cube gallery and great restaurants like Casse Croute and José Pizarro, it’s an apt home for a wine school. WSET is the global standard for booze qualifications. It offers classes in beers, sake and spirits, but wine is its bread and butter. Sommeliers from top restaurants around the world will study here for years to get the highest qualification: a Level Four Diploma. Next time you’re at a fancy restaurant, look out for the little pin badges proudly displayed by somms who have put in PhD-level graft. 

My own ambitions were more modest, namely, a full-day course to get my Level One (the difficulty between levels rises exponentially). Arriving in the morning to the classroom felt like going back to school, only here the desks were covered in wine glasses rather than pencil shavings. My class of 20 or so was pretty mixed. A WSET spokesperson explains that one of the biggest changes the school has seen since Covid is the rise of amateur enthusiasts taking courses rather than just people in hospitality and the drinks sector more widely. In my group there was one man who loved wine and had brought his mate who had “nothing better to do” on a Friday; a couple of friends wanting to order better wine when they hit the town; one guy was plotting a coup to become head bartender; a husband wanted to catch up to his Level Three wife; and some of the younger members of the class looked like their parents may have bought them the course for Christmas. 

The day is split into two halves: theory in the morning and tasting in the afternoon (you can also do Level One across two evening classes). Our teacher, who was knowledgeable and enthusiastic, took us through the basics of wine production, grape characteristics, different styles, best practices with serving, drinking and storing. It was genuinely fun, and although never super challenging, by lunchtime we could read a wine list and know more or less what to expect from the bottle. 

During the lunch break I was so geed-up on wine learning that I went and spent a small fortune on bottles of wine from 40 Maltby Street. Sadly my words failed me when met with the incredibly cool, natural wine connoisseurs working there. 

The afternoon session is a little blurrier. Spitting was encouraged, but not enforced. It was an amazing experience to taste along with a sommelier as they throw out words that in that exact sip, makes total sense: green pepper, Haribo, stewed plums, Petits Filous yoghurt, apricot, clove, menthol cigarettes, tarte Tatin, black olives and manure. Our teacher told us that one of the best ways to develop your palate is just to smell everything you come across, which I’ve been doing – slightly deranged baby-esque – ever since. 

The Level One course was a gentle expanding of what wine can be – and how it doesn’t always need to adhere to rigid rules. At the end of the day you take an exam, which also reminded me of going back to school in a less good way with its big ticking clock and candidate numbers. Had I known it was exam conditions, I might have gone lighter in the sampling. But brimming with overconfidence I breezed through and got an email a couple of weeks later confirming I’d passed – not, however, without a few mistakes.

Not to worry, it just gives me something to aim for when I take my Level Two. 

Want to learn more about wine? Here’s a breakdown of the qualifications run by WSET:

  • At Level 1, you’ll learn the fundamentals in an approachable way, helping you explore and enjoy drinks with greater confidence.  
  • At Level 2, that confidence grows into broader knowledge and understanding. You’ll learn to compare products, understand how production influences style and quality, and develop a more structured approach to tasting and evaluation.

It’s baffling that sport’s global leaders are still prevaricating over Russia as the LA28 Olympics and Paralympics draw ever nearer, says Ed Warner.

To Brentford FC’s Gtech Community Stadium last week for the second outing of The NEDwork, a gathering of chairs and non-executive directors from across Great Britain’s Olympic and Paralympic governing bodies. 

Russia’s return to the Games, and the chaotic way in which it is being handled, was the principal concern of the chairs of Britain’s OLY and PLY sports when I spoke to them. Specifically, the inconsistent approaches of the IOC, the IPC and the individual international sport federations that control their component sports.

Eleven years on from the eruption of Russia’s doping scandal and four and a half years after its invasion of Ukraine, it is baffling that the rulers of global sport are still unable to agree on a coherent response to these twin severe challenges that President Putin’s regime has posed to its moral code.

Remember the hole in the wall at the Sochi 2014 anti-doping lab? Well, this still stands as a shocking totem of the systemic doping that drove a wedge between the IOC and key affected sports, especially athletics. 

It also divided the Olympic and Paralympic movements – the IPC adopting a tougher stance towards Russian participation at Rio 2016 and jeopardising its financial and operational dependence on the IOC as a result.

Initial responses to the war in Ukraine were largely uniform, matching the watching world’s condemnation of Putin’s assault. In time, though, the outright ban on Russian athletes has steadily eroded. 

That may be the result of simple fatigue, the nagging caution of legal advisors, the softer stance of Russia’s natural allies or realpolitik from those anxious to court favour with President Trump ahead of the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Whatever the mix of forces, sport’s attitude to Russian participation in international events ranges widely. Athletics still won’t allow it (having for a while, pre-war, softened its position to allow heavily-tested athletes to compete as “neutrals”); a string of sports permit selected Russian neutrals without their national flag or anthem; the IPC has swung from hardline to soft and beat the IOC to full restoration of rights; and the IOC has shifted in the same direction but is hiding behind the line that it is up to individual sports to decide.

With all due respect to the Paralympics – and I write as chair of GB Wheelchair Rugby, albeit in a personal capacity here – it is the IOC’s morphing position that has caused such angst, not just in Britain but much more widely. 

The organisation’s presidential baton passed from Thomas Bach to Kirsty Coventry in 2025. Both are arch pragmatists keen at all times to court approbation across the globe, and conscious that success in IOC elections rests on garnering votes from the many smaller nations rather than the wealthy few.

Map a one-member, one-vote organisational democracy against Russia’s spheres of influence and it becomes easy to understand why Western European arguments in favour of sporting sanctions carry less sway than their proponents might hope or expect. The old adage about the value of seeing things from your opponent’s perspective holds true. Little wonder many administrators end up feeling impotent.

It is hard to know whether individual sports are providing leadership to the IOC on the Russia question, or vice versa. What we do know is that judo, taekwondo, aquatics and fencing, for example, now allow the full flummery of national kit, flags and anthem as well as Russian athletes themselves. Still no place for senior Russian football teams, though, given that Fifa’s ban remains.

“We are determined to ensure that pools and open water remain places where athletes from all nations can come together in peaceful competition.”

Kuwait’s Husain Al-Musallam, President of World Aquatics, April 2026

Much of the agonising by Britain‘s governing bodies over Russia stems from their duties to the athletes who compete for Team GB and ParalympicsGB. In part, this has an eye on the make-up of the competition and GB medal prospects; but more significantly this reflects the realisation that athletes are the people who will be in the media spotlight at Games time. Their soundbites will be the ones that reverberate. Any decision to shake hands or share a podium would constitute a propaganda photo op for the Russian regime.

If you doubt how tricky this might be, just consider the moral knot that Irish football has tied itself up in recently. Two men’s Nations League matches have taken place between the Republic of Ireland and Israel in neutral venues, the Irish team coming under intense pressure at home to take a stance against Israeli actions in Gaza. 

The players found themselves in an invidious position when presumably all they want to do is pursue their sporting ambitions. Whether their football association and Uefa did right by them is up for debate, your own stance likely depending on your view of the Gaza conflict.

Multiply this situation – by no means black and white – by the number of athletes who might compete against Russians and Belarusians at LA28 and you can see that the opportunity for noise, uncertainty and grandstanding is enormous. A media godsend, although possibly the sheer quantity of stories will dull their edge as the twin Games progress.

It is by no means clear that Donald Trump would want to welcome Russian athletes to LA28 with full team accoutrements, but his current rhetoric about the war in Ukraine might suggest that Russia’s participation would carry a symbolism consistent with his desire to force conflict resolution.

”I am optimistic about further progress that would establish a reliable mechanism for fuller participation by Russian athletes at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.”

US President Trump’s special envoy, Paolo Zampolli, interviewed by TASS last week. The next day he announced he’d left his post

With the Games still the best part of two years away, you might assume there is plenty of time for this issue to be resolved, but that is to ignore qualification processes that will begin in earnest next year. 

The IOC’s softer stance was announced too close to this year’s Winter Olympics to make much difference to the number of Russian and Belarusian athletes who took part. With the much greater profile and scale of a Summer Games, those advocating inclusion will be aware they need to push hard now if they are to secure a near full-strength Russian presence in LA.

Whatever the outcome, there will be athletes put on the spot and asked to take a stance either way, Ukrainians included. Each deserves leaders prepared to provide moral cover, not so that they can shelve their own consciences, but because true responsibility should lie with those in charge of global sport who have abdicated that responsibility so abjectly to date.

Ed Warner is chair of Sussex Cricket and GB Wheelchair Rugby and writes his sport column at sportinc.substack.com

    Since coming to power, Labour has passed some hefty laws, including its landmark renters’ rights reform and employment overhaul, but they aren’t giving voters more power; they’re passing them onto the already backlogged Tribunal system, writes Maria Ward-Brennan.

    One of the main reforms in focus is the Renters’ Rights Act, which came into force in May. This has led to the overhaul of tenant protections, including abolishing no-fault evictions, replacing fixed-term contracts with rolling periodic tenancies, and effectively ending rent increases. However, some economists have questioned the Act’s effectiveness and raised concerns that the reforms would actually harm renters in the long run.

    Valentin Boboc, senior economist at the Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA), told City AM: “Landlords are more likely to quit when letting becomes less profitable and more uncertain. Policies such as creating an increasingly lengthy and uncertain tribunal process [for rent reviews] or imposing onerous costs, may lead more landlords to sell their properties, thereby reducing the availability of rental accommodation.”

    However, another concern is the pressure these changes will put on the country’s legal system.

    The housing minister, Matthew Pennycook MP, posted on social media on Tuesday that the Labour government’s Renters’ Rights Act “empowers private renters to challenge unreasonable rent increases”, adding that Brits can now refer the matter to the First-Tier Tribunal (FTT). He shared a link to a recent legal judgment in his post on X in which someone challenged their landlord in court over a rent increase, only to have the rent reduced – by more than the proposed increase.

    On top of warning against bringing the courts into it, Silvia Andreoletti, head of communications at the Adam Smith Institute, told City AM, “setting rents through Tribunals rather than the free market is a policy bound to fail.”

    Surge in Tribunal cases

    The major problem with the government’s bold vision is that it pushes people toward Tribunals, which are already backlogged or at risk of becoming backlogged because of the increased workload as a result of these new reforms.

    Rent cases go to the First-tier Tribunal, Property Chambers, which has reportedly already seen a surge in cases. As the Act came into force in May, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said the first complete three-month period (quarter) in which the new rules were fully in effect across all cases was July to September, and those figures will be published in December.

    Andreoletti added that as “almost three-quarters of Tribunals find in favour of the tenant”, she added, “any rational tenant would jump at the opportunity to take any [rent] increase to Tribunal.”

    The government was questioned on this matter earlier this year. Sarah Sackman MP reassured Parliament that while the MoJ expects more cases due to housing reforms, the department is managing it through digital upgrades and by centralising staff for Tribunals.

    As of April 2026, the MoJ has 112 judges sitting in the First-Tier Tribunal (Property Chamber).

    A government spokesperson told City AM: “Our Renters’ Rights Act empowers tenants to challenge unreasonable rent increases, with a recent Manchester case seeing a tribunal determine that the market rate was £200 below the landlord’s proposed level. 

    “We are supporting all courts and tribunals to cope with potential additional pressure by maximising sitting days and continuing to invest in the annual recruitment of up to 1,000 judges and tribunal members across all jurisdictions.”

    Employment Tribunal on the brink

    But it seems to be the solution for all its major overhauls. The government’s major change to employment rights law is now putting severe pressure on the Employment Tribunal, which was already suffering from a backlog formed during the pandemic.

    The latest figures show that the Employment Tribunal backlog has hit record highs, with around 70,000 to 77,594 open single claims and over 467,000 total open cases. Lawyers have said some case listings in parts of London and the South East Tribunals stretch into 2028, 2029, and even 2030.

    Employment lawyers have been vocal about how strained the Tribunal is, and predictions suggest the pressure will worsen as Employment Rights Act rights, which are spaced out over the next couple of years, all come into force.

    Tribunal judges are beginning to face battles over how to handle the surge of AI-generated claims submitted by people, including lengthy grievances that contain hallucinations, which is starting to overwhelm the legal system and add even more delays to the already established backlog.

    They said they believe it is “definitely a US firm” and have reportedly heard it will be Willkie Farr & Gallagher or Skadden, both New York-headquartered white-shoe law firms.     Vinson & Elkins is another large US firm known for its work in the energy sector. With global revenues of $1.11bn, the firm is headquartered in Houston, Texas, where Weil has three established offices, a State that is a US energy powerhouse.

    Labour may have approved the Jackdaw gas field, but it is still set on destroying our industrial base to save the planet. It’s another to engage in unilateral economic disarmament so China can sell us the cars we used to build. We must reverse this madness, licence drilling in the North Sea, and make energy abundant again, says Richard Tice

    At long last, Andy Burnham has had a good idea: lifting a policy from Reform UK. We’re delighted that the Prime Minister has seen the sense of our push to approve drilling at the Jackdaw gas field. If he’d like, we’d be happy to take some other decisions for him too.

    We could start with Rosebank. Jackdaw is an important first step in reversing Labour’s deliberate destruction of our North Sea industry, and towards energy security, but it is only that. The Rosebank oil and gas field could replace five per cent of Britain’s energy imports. Together, at peak, they’ll reach eight per cent: vital security of supply in a dangerous world. 

    Undoubtedly, the net stupid zero zealots will start dooming and glooming at this point: “It’s only eight per cent”. But the point is that – apart from the billions in revenues for the treasury, the jobs, the support for the pound, and the security of supply – these fields are almost ready to go. And with a bit of smart thinking, we can push much further. 

    Billions of barrels

    There are billions of barrels of oil, and their equivalent in gas, lying beneath the North Sea. There is an expert, world-leading industry, developed here in Britain, which wants to drill it. And there are British households who are preparing to spend a cold winter shivering in their homes because of high energy prices. 

    The Labour party thinks this is perfectly fine. They’re happy for you to be cold to save the planet. China, meanwhile, is opening 85 new coal power plants this year: twice as much capacity as Britain’s entire renewables sector can realistically provide. 

    It’s one thing to destroy your industrial base to save the planet. It’s another to engage in unilateral economic disarmament so China can sell us the cars we used to build. We must reverse this madness, licence drilling in the North Sea, and make energy abundant again. 

    I’ve pledged to cut bills by £250 in our first 100 days in office. And if I don’t achieve it, I’ll resign

    We must also make energy cheaper. Energy is prosperity. Expensive energy means less heavy industry, no manufacturing revival, a weakened chemical industry, and colder, darker homes. Andy Burnham should take a leaf out of our book: make the VAT cut on energy bills permanent, scrap the Emissions Trading Scheme and Carbon Price Support taxes, and take the costs of green boondoggles into general taxation while working to scrap them permanently. Together, these steps will cut energy bills by £250, boosting growth and living standards.

    Now, the zealots will claim that it’s impossible to do anything quickly, and that you just have to put up with the misery. Absolute nonsense. If Burnham got into gear today, everything I’ve laid out could be achieved by the end of January – when the price cap is currently set to skyrocket £276. And I mean this: I’ve pledged to cut bills by £250 in our first 100 days in office. And if I don’t achieve it, I’ll resign. 

    Regrettably, this is probably wishful thinking. The Labour party is utterly in thrall to net zero, which is why Burnham dithered for so long over Jackdaw in the first place. I’m afraid this brief flash of common sense will be just that: momentary sanity from a party committed to madness. It will take a change of government to give the country a pathway back to an energy policy that will keep the lights on and the bills down.

    And if Andy Burnham wants to test the popularity of his ideas in an election, we’re more than ready. Britain is broken. Britain needs Reform.

    Richard Tice is business, trade and energy spokesman for Reform UK
