]]> Supercomputer set to take AI to the Moon aboard Astrolab rover https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/supercomputer-ai-moon-aboard-astrolab-rover/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:48:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54243 Hewlett Packard Enterprise is preparing to send its Spaceborne Computer-4 to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s FLIP rover.

The post Supercomputer set to take AI to the Moon aboard Astrolab rover appeared first on AGN.

]]> A supercomputer capable of running artificial intelligence, including large language models, is preparing to travel to the Moon aboard a robotic rover later this year, in an experiment that could allow future lunar missions to analyse information and make decisions without constantly relying on controllers on Earth.

The Spaceborne Computer-4, developed by Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), is one of approximately 20 scientific and technology payloads aboard Astrolab’s 480 kg FLIP lunar rover, which is being prepared for launch as early as November. 

What will the FLIP lunar rover do on the Moon?

Alongside experiments involving artificial intelligence and advanced computing, the rover will carry instruments to map the lunar surface and investigate its composition.

The computer will attempt the first high-performance computing benchmarks on the lunar surface, alongside experiments involving AI-powered image analysis, navigation, document searches and cybersecurity.

The aim is to demonstrate that complex computing tasks normally performed in laboratories or data centres on Earth can be carried out directly on the Moon.

That capability could become increasingly important as NASA and commercial companies prepare for more frequent lunar missions, including operations in which robots must work for long periods without astronauts present.

HPE President and CEO Antonio Neri emphasised the importance of processing information directly on the Moon rather than relying entirely on computing facilities on Earth.

“As lunar activity accelerates, the ability to process data where it’s created will be critical to unlocking new scientific insights and supporting autonomous, sustained operations,” Neri wrote on LinkedIn.

He highlighted the company’s collaboration with NASA, the International Space Station National Laboratory, Astrolab, KIOXIA and Deloitte on the mission.

Scott Wiest, HPE’s vice president, fellow and global sales chief technologist said, “The next chapter of lunar exploration will depend on the ability to turn data into insights at the point of discovery.”

“With HPE Spaceborne Computer-4, we are bringing AI and high-performance computing to the lunar edge, helping the acceleration of scientific discovery and building the infrastructure for the next era of exploration,” Wiest added.

The mission is expected to launch in November 2026 under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative. Its success, including the computer’s performance in the lunar environment, remains to be demonstrated.

Why take a supercomputer to the Moon?

Spacecraft traditionally collect information and transmit much of it to Earth, where engineers and scientists analyse the results and send instructions back.

That approach works, but communications take time and bandwidth is limited. The difficulty becomes greater as missions travel further from Earth.

A computer capable of processing images, identifying hazards and interpreting scientific observations directly aboard a rover could reduce the amount of information that must be transmitted.

This approach is known as edge computing: instead of sending everything to a distant data centre, information is processed close to where it is collected.

HPE’s system will combine a central processing unit, or CPU, with a graphics processing unit, or GPU. The CPU handles general computing tasks, while the GPU can perform many calculations simultaneously, making it useful for AI and image processing.

High-performance computing, or HPC, refers to using substantial computing power to solve complex problems. On FLIP, the objective is not to reproduce a large terrestrial supercomputer, but to test advanced computing workloads using a compact module designed for space.

The distinction is important. The planned lunar experiments will assess whether such technology can operate reliably under conditions that are very different from those on Earth.

AI that can read, analyse and navigate

Among the experiments planned for the mission are specialised large language models, or LLMs, the type of AI technology used in conversational systems.

On the Moon, their role will be different from answering everyday questions.

The models will be tested on tasks such as searching technical documents, interpreting information and helping researchers make sense of data collected by the rover.

HPE also plans to process images and measurements from LiDAR, a laser-based system that measures distances to surrounding objects and builds three-dimensional maps. Such information could help a rover recognise obstacles, understand the terrain and identify safer routes.

NASA will contribute two AI experiments. One, called Federated Learning for Unbounded and Intelligent Decentralization (FLUID), will demonstrate coordination between three AI models using data associated with Earth, the Moon and the International Space Station.

The other will test a specially adapted language model that can search and interpret documents stored aboard the spacecraft.

Deloitte will contribute Silent Shield, a system intended to identify unusual computer activity and potential cyber intrusions.

The experiments are demonstrations, not evidence that an AI system is ready to control future lunar missions independently.

Surviving the lunar environment

Running advanced computing equipment on the Moon presents difficulties that do not exist inside an ordinary data centre.

There is almost no atmosphere to carry away heat, temperatures vary enormously between sunlit and shaded areas, and electronics are exposed to radiation.

HPE has designed Spaceborne Computer-4 as a lightweight, self-contained unit without conventional cooling fans. It will use the rover’s thermal management system to help control its temperature.

The module includes low-power processors and solid-state storage supplied by KIOXIA. Unlike traditional hard drives, solid-state drives have no moving parts.

HPE is also using software to protect the computer against radiation-related disturbances.

As MIT Technology Review reported on 20 October, the company’s approach builds on earlier Spaceborne computers tested aboard the International Space Station. The software monitors the system for problems and can reduce processing speed and power when radiation conditions become hazardous.

HPE chief scientist and principal investigator Mark Fernandez explained the difficulty of operating equipment that cannot be repaired easily.

“In space, we don’t have the redundancy, we don’t have the repairman, we don’t have the spare parts,” he said, according to MIT Technology Review.

The company has previously flown three generations of Spaceborne computers to the ISS. The programme has demonstrated that commercially derived computing hardware can operate in space with appropriate protection.

In 2025, the ISS programme also tested Meta’s Llama 3.2 language model as part of the Space Llama initiative.

The Moon presents a tougher test because the equipment will operate outside the comparatively controlled environment of a crewed space station.

Astrolab’s rover and the Artemis connection

The computer will travel aboard FLIP, short for FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform, an approximately 480-kilogram robotic rover developed by California-based Venturi Astrolab.

FLIP is intended to carry around 20 scientific and technology payloads, including equipment for mapping the lunar surface and investigating the composition of lunar soil.

The rover uses specialised deformable wheels designed to maintain traction on uneven terrain.

It is scheduled to be delivered near the lunar south pole aboard the Griffin-1 lander, part of NASA’s CLPS programme, which purchases lunar delivery services from commercial companies.

Astrolab founder and chief executive Jaret Matthews said the rover would provide an opportunity to test technologies under actual lunar conditions.

“Our FLIP rover is designed to accommodate a variety of payloads, and this mission will demonstrate how commercial lunar mobility platforms can support technology development and scientific research.”

Astrolab also has a separate role in NASA’s Artemis lunar exploration programme.

In May 2026, NASA selected the company as one of two providers of crewed lunar rovers under its revised surface mobility plans.

The approximately $219 million task order covers development and delivery of the CLV-1 vehicle, which is intended to transport astronauts and equipment around the lunar south pole.

CLV-1 is a different vehicle from FLIP. It is designed to carry astronauts, while FLIP is an uncrewed technology and science platform.

The crewed rover draws on Astrolab’s FLEX architecture and technology developed with Venturi Space, including wheels, batteries and battery management systems.

NASA expects the newly contracted crewed vehicles to reach the Moon by 2028.

NASA is already using AI to study the Moon

The planned computing experiment comes as NASA expands the use of artificial intelligence in lunar research.

In September, NASA and IBM released a Lunar Foundation Model trained primarily on images collected by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

The model was developed using roughly two million image tiles, including more than one million high-resolution camera images and nearly 964,000 multispectral images.

Researchers can adapt it to identify craters, investigate volcanic features and estimate where ice might remain stable near the lunar poles.

Kevin Murphy, NASA’s chief science data officer and acting chief data and AI officer, said the challenge was making decades of observations easier to use.

“We also have to make data easier for scientists to explore and use,” he said.

Unlike HPE’s proposed lunar experiment, the NASA-IBM model is designed for scientific analysis rather than specifically for operation aboard FLIP. Both developments, however, reflect growing interest in using AI to extract useful information from large quantities of space data.

From experiment to future lunar operations

The immediate objective for HPE is to establish that advanced computing can function reliably on the lunar surface.

Its planned tests include two established computing benchmarks, High Performance LINPACK and High Performance Conjugate Gradient, which measure different aspects of a computer’s ability to perform demanding calculations.

HPE will also support Astrolab’s mission control in Hawthorne, California, using its private cloud and operations software.

]]> Lockheed Martin and Department of War unveil framework for 850 F-35 fighter jets https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/lockheed-martin-department-of-war-850-f-35-fighter-jets/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:05:54 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54254 The Department of War and Lockheed Martin have unveiled a decade-long framework covering at least 850 F-35 fighter jets, alongside sustainment, upgrades and international orders worth billions.

The post Lockheed Martin and Department of War unveil framework for 850 F-35 fighter jets appeared first on AGN.

]]> Lockheed Martin has unveiled a long-term framework agreement with the Department of War that lays the groundwork for the procurement and support of at least 850 F-35 Lightning II aircraft over the next 10 years.

The proposed arrangement spans production Lots 21-30 and includes not only aircraft procurement but also initial spares, modification kits, and a decade of sustainment support.

International customer orders are also expected to be folded into the framework. Production will continue at the programme’s current rate of 156 aircraft per year.

The agreement is not yet a formal aircraft order. Final contract pricing, schedules and quantities will depend on Congress granting multi-year procurement authority and the associated funding approvals in the coming months.

Why the F-35 programme is changing

For years, the F-35 programme has operated under annual contracting cycles, creating uncertainty for suppliers and limiting opportunities for long-term investment. The new framework is designed to change that.

“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” said Lockheed Martin Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet.

“With the greater certainty that comes from the US government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain.”

The company argues that securing demand years in advance will enable suppliers to purchase raw materials and components in larger volumes, reducing lead times and easing pressure on the defence industrial base.

Lower costs and higher readiness

Improving fleet readiness is a central objective of the framework.

“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” said OJ Sanchez, president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.

“This, in addition to the investments Lockheed Martin is making to the global spares pool, will directly translate into higher mission capable rates and a more resilient supply chain.”

Boost for the US economy

The company estimates the framework will support approximately 317,000 US jobs and generate around $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade.

Lockheed has also committed to self-funding at least $7 billion in initiatives that support the F-35 programme.

More than 1,375 F-35s are currently in service worldwide, with the fleet surpassing one million flight hours. The aircraft now operates from 42 bases globally, including in 13 nations flying the type from home territory.

As the world’s largest fighter programme looks to its next decade, the proposed framework is intended to provide something the F-35 enterprise has long sought: stability, scale and predictability for manufacturers, operators and suppliers alike.

]]> F-117 Nighthawk: Restored legendary stealth aircraft joins the Smithsonian Collection https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/restored-lockheed-f117-smithsonian-collection/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:14:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54177 With its stealth capabilities, the selected aircraft has a remarkable operational record, having flown live missions in four major conflicts.

The post F-117 Nighthawk: Restored legendary stealth aircraft joins the Smithsonian Collection appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Lockheed F-117A Nighthawk, one of the most revolutionary military aircraft ever developed, is preparing to take its place among aviation history’s most significant machines at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Air and Space Museum.

Nicknamed ‘The Overachiever’, the aircraft (serial number #818) has a remarkable operational record, having flown combat missions in all four major conflicts in which the F-117 participated.

The US Air Force (USAF) transferred the aircraft (serial number 818) to the museum in October 2026, following an announcement by Lockheed Martin and the Smithsonian in September.

After restoration and reassembly, it is expected to go on public display at the museum’s Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Centre in Chantilly, Virginia, near Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

A unique aircraft with a remarkable history

The F-117A Nighthawk holds a special place in military aviation as the world’s first operational stealth combat aircraft.

Developed in secrecy by Lockheed’s celebrated Skunk Works division, it introduced a new approach to aerial warfare, allowing the USAF to attack heavily defended targets while greatly reducing the likelihood of detection by enemy radar.

Aircraft 818 joining the Smithsonian collection is particularly significant. Known as The Overachiever, it is the only F-117 documented as having flown combat missions in all four major conflicts involving the type – Operation Just Cause in Panama in 1989, Operation Desert Storm in Iraq in 1991, Operation Allied Force over Yugoslavia in 1999, and Operation Iraqi Freedom in Iraq in 2003.

Its service during the 1991 Gulf War helped establish the F-117’s legendary reputation. Nighthawks penetrated Iraqi airspace to strike strategically important targets, including command facilities and air-defence installations.

Their ability to approach targets with a reduced radar signature gave commanders an important new option at the opening of an air campaign.

According to US military reporting, the featured aircraft flew 1,271 sorties during its participation in the 1991 conflict, achieving an 80% mission success rate without sustaining battle damage.

What was the F-117 Nighthawk?

Despite its official F-117 designation, the Nighthawk was not a conventional fighter designed to engage enemy aircraft in air-to-air combat.

It was a specialised, single-seat attack aircraft developed primarily to penetrate defended airspace and destroy high-value ground targets.

Its development began during the 1970s, when the US military sought ways to counter increasingly capable radar-guided surface-to-air missile systems.

Lockheed’s Skunk Works developed an aircraft whose distinctive angular surfaces helped deflect radar waves away from their source. Radar-absorbent materials further reduced its visibility to enemy detection systems.

The result was an aircraft that looked unlike anything previously seen in operational military service. Its sharply faceted black exterior, unusual planform and carefully shaped surfaces were designed around stealth rather than conventional aerodynamic elegance.

The F-117 first flew in 1981 and achieved initial operational capability in 1983. Its existence remained classified for years, with the US government publicly acknowledging the programme in 1988. The aircraft made its first formal public appearance in 1990.

Although the F-117 was officially designated a fighter, its actual role was precision ground attack. It was used to destroy command-and-control facilities, air-defence systems and other strategically important targets, often operating at night to further reduce the risk of detection.

When was the F-117 retired?

The US Air Force officially retired the F-117 fleet in 2008, following more than two decades of service. Its pioneering capabilities had helped pave the way for newer stealth platforms, including the B-2 Spirit bomber and the F-22 Raptor.

The F-35 Lightning II also belongs to the wider generation of aircraft benefiting from advances in low-observable technology.

Retirement did not mean the immediate disappearance of every Nighthawk. Some aircraft remained in storage and selected examples continued to appear in training and test activities after the fleet’s formal withdrawal from operational service.

For The Overachiever, the move to the Smithsonian represents a new chapter. Before its transfer, Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works team prepared the aircraft for public exhibition, removing sensitive military equipment and making the necessary changes to preserve its appearance without exposing classified technology.

Its wings and fuselage were transported separately aboard a USAF C-5M Super Galaxy before being delivered to Virginia.

Preserving a milestone in aviation history

The National Air and Space Museum’s acquisition ensures that visitors will be able to examine one of the aircraft that transformed modern military aviation up close.

The Udvar-Hazy Centre, located near Washington Dulles International Airport, houses a substantial collection of historic aircraft and spacecraft. The Nighthawk’s arrival adds an important example of the technological changes that shaped air power at the end of the Cold War and beyond.

For aviation enthusiasts, The Overachiever is more than an unusually shaped aircraft. It represents the moment when stealth moved from an experimental concept to a practical combat capability, changing how military aircraft were designed and how air campaigns could be conducted.

Once hidden behind layers of secrecy, the F-117 will now be preserved for the public as a landmark in aerospace engineering. Its transition from frontline attack aircraft to museum exhibit provides a fitting tribute to a machine whose influence extends well beyond its years in active service.

]]> Airbus predicts demand for 2,670 freighters as global air cargo fleet grows 46% https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airbus-predicts-demand-2670-freighters/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 11:51:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54208 In its 2026 Cargo Global Market Forecast, Airbus said the dedicated freighter fleet would grow by 46% by 2045.

The post Airbus predicts demand for 2,670 freighters as global air cargo fleet grows 46% appeared first on AGN.

]]> Airbus expects demand for 2,670 freighter aircraft over the next two decades, as airlines and cargo operators replace ageing aircraft and respond to growing demand for air freight.

In its 2026 Cargo Global Market Forecast, published on 21 October, the manufacturer said the dedicated freighter fleet would grow by 46% from around 2,360 aircraft in 2026 to 3,460 aircraft by 2045.

Of the 2,670 aircraft required, Airbus forecasts that 1,700 will come from passenger-to-freighter conversions, while 970 will be newly built freighters.

Why airlines are converting passenger jets into cargo aircraft

Rather than purchasing a new aircraft, operators can give an existing passenger jet a second life by transforming its cabin into a cargo compartment.

This involves modifications including reinforced floors, cargo loading doors and systems designed to carry freight.

Airbus offers passenger-to-freighter conversion options across its A320, A321 and A330 families, providing operators with aircraft for different cargo needs.

The company’s previous forecast estimated 1,670 conversions over a 20-year period to 2044, compared with 935 newly manufactured freighters.

Airbus A350F targets long-haul cargo flights

Alongside converted aircraft, Airbus is developing the A350F for the long-haul cargo sector.

The company said it had secured 34 orders for the aircraft this year and that certification activity with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) was progressing.

The A350F completed its maiden flight on 29 September, marking a key milestone for the programme. Airbus is aiming to strengthen its position in the large widebody freighter segment, a market long dominated by Boeing.

Designed to carry up to 111 tonnes of freight, the A350F has a range of 8,700km and features an electrically operated main-deck cargo door. At 4.3m wide, Airbus says it is the industry’s largest main-deck cargo door.

The aircraft is designed to accommodate standard containers and pallets, as well as oversized cargo including large aircraft engines.

According to Airbus, the A350F will deliver lower fuel burn and CO₂ emissions than previous-generation freighters.

Where will the new freighters go?

North America and Asia-Pacific are expected to account for almost two-thirds of global demand, requiring 925 and 850 aircraft respectively.

Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) are forecast to require 515 aircraft, followed by Latin America (165), the Middle East (125) and Africa (90).

Airbus expects Asia-Pacific to remain the world’s largest international air freight market, with traffic between Asia-Pacific and North America forecast to be the fastest-growing major corridor, expanding by 3.8% annually.

What’s driving growth in air cargo demand?

The rise of online shopping, expanding global trade and demand for faster deliveries are expected to support growth in air cargo traffic over the next two decades. Freight aircraft play an important role in moving time-sensitive and high-value goods, from consumer electronics and pharmaceuticals to industrial equipment and aircraft parts.

Airbus believes this growth, combined with the retirement of older aircraft, will create demand for thousands of additional freighters.

]]> Gulfstream targets production of 200 private jets a year as orders surge https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/gulfstream-production-200-private-jets-orders/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 11:03:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54191 Gulfstream has seen sustained demand for its large-cabin business jets, particularly the G500, G600, G700 and G800.

The post Gulfstream targets production of 200 private jets a year as orders surge appeared first on AGN.

]]> Gulfstream Aerospace plans to produce at least 200 private jets annually. The US business jet manufacturer expects to build around 160 aircraft this year, but believes its factories can support higher production rates.

Speaking at the NBAA Business Aviation Convention & Exhibition (NBAA-BACE) in Las Vegas, Gulfstream president Mark Burns said demand justified increasing output.

“Demand is not the concern right now. If we can build more aeroplanes tonight, we can sell more aeroplanes today,” Burns told reporters, as reported by Aviation Week.

The company expects production to increase during 2027, 2028 and 2029, although it has not announced a firm date for reaching its target of 200 aircraft annually.

Gulfstream backlog exceeds $25 billion

Gulfstream has seen sustained demand for its large-cabin business jets, particularly the G500, G600, G700 and G800.

The manufacturer’s order backlog exceeded $25 billion by mid-2026, up about $4 billion from late 2025, according to Aviation International News. 

In its financial results published in July, Gulfstream’s parent company, General Dynamics, reported aerospace orders of $5.3 billion in the second quarter of 2026. The company reported $3.5 billion in aerospace revenue, up 15.1% from the previous year.

Gulfstream delivered 41 aircraft during the quarter, compared with 38 in the same period of 2025. Deliveries for the first six months reached 79 aircraft, up from 74 a year earlier.

New Gulfstream aircraft support production growth

Gulfstream’s production plans centre on a family of six business jets developed over the past decade.

Four models are already in service, while the G400 large-cabin jet and G300 super-midsize aircraft are progressing through development and flight testing.

The G700 received certification in March 2024, followed by the longer-range G800 in April 2025.

Burns said Gulfstream had delivered 135 G700 aircraft and 35 G800s. Deliveries of the G600 and G500 have each reached around 200 aircraft.

The manufacturer has invested in two production campuses in Savannah, Georgia, with assembly facilities designed to accommodate different aircraft models according to demand.

One campus supports G700 and G800 production, while the other accommodates the G400, G500 and G600.

The facilities were designed with additional capacity, allowing Gulfstream to increase output without requiring an entirely new production system.

Burns said the company already had the capacity to manufacture more than 200 wing sets annually.

Supply chain recovery allows Gulfstream to plan higher output

Gulfstream also expects fewer supply chain constraints as it increases production.

“I don’t see the supply chain as limiting us today. I think we will see growth in 2027, 2028 and 2029,” Burns told Aviation Week.

The manufacturer has produced its own wings since 2014 and is considering bringing additional manufacturing activities in-house.

The approach would give Gulfstream greater control over components that previously caused production delays, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.

However, increasing aircraft assembly rates also requires additional capacity for cabin completion, deliveries and customer support.

Gulfstream is expanding its global spare parts network and maintenance capabilities to accommodate its growing fleet.

According to Aviation International News, the manufacturer has invested approximately $3 billion in spare parts inventory and operates 12 distribution centres worldwide.

The company has also expanded its Atlanta distribution facility and increased component repair capabilities in the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

Gulfstream expects further growth through 2029

Moving from 160 aircraft annually to 200 would represent a 25% increase in production.

It would also establish a new annual manufacturing rate for Gulfstream, supported by its expanded product range and existing order backlog.

The company has not committed to a specific production timetable, but Burns expressed confidence that the increase would happen.

“Barring any unforeseen catastrophe, I think it’s inevitable,” he said.

For Gulfstream, the immediate priority is increasing production of its certified aircraft while completing development of the G400 and G300.

Both aircraft will broaden the manufacturer’s portfolio and create additional growth opportunities as production capacity increases.

]]> Europe considers giving private companies powers to shoot down drones https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/europe-private-cuas-critical-infrastructure/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 10:27:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54160 Growing concern over drone activity near critical infrastructure is prompting some European governments to consider expanding who can respond, including allowing approved private operators to use counter-drone measures.

The post Europe considers giving private companies powers to shoot down drones appeared first on AGN.

]]> The rapid spread of drone technology is forcing governments to rethink who is responsible for protecting critical infrastructure.

According to a new Reuters report, several European countries are considering giving critical-infrastructure operators greater powers to counter drone threats, including measures traditionally reserved for state authorities.

As concerns grow over unauthorised drone activity near power plants, airports and other sensitive sites, governments are grappling with how to protect an expanding number of potential targets while ensuring any new powers are subject to clear legal safeguards and oversight.

Why European states are considering allowing companies to shoot down drones

In late 2024 and 2025, a series of drone incursions over military sites in Europe and the United States highlighted legal and operational constraints on responding to civilian drones during peacetime.

Since then, a range of measures have been introduced, including in the UK, where the military has been granted greater authority to respond to suspected drone threats.

Now, some governments are considering whether operators of critical infrastructure and their contractors should be allowed to play a more active role in defending key sites against potential drone attacks.

European governments are increasingly concerned about the risk of hybrid attacks targeting critical infrastructure, including those linked to Russia.

Kristian Ruby, secretary general of European energy body Eurelectric, said, “It is a theoretical, and increasingly a practical, possibility that there could be heating outages this winter due to hybrid attacks.”

Legality questions need to be solved first

Various legal issues need to be worked out across Europe, as the rapid emergence of drone threats and the ensuing countermeasures are moving faster than relevant laws and regulations.

European countries are having to solve issues like who has the right to respond to a drone threat and what liability there may be for injury and property damage from downed drones. These legal issues are important for many companies before they start shooting down drones.

Some start-ups, like  Impact Drones, are building their business model around these trends and are developing counter-UAS solutions for critical infrastructure operators (e.g., data centres).

Russia has been forced down this road even faster. In March 2026, Putin signed legislation allowing private security organisations to protect critical energy infrastructure using firearms. In May, Moscow allowed them to acquire anti-aircraft artillery, gun turrets, radar, and EW equipment.

With the Wagner revolt of 2023 still fresh in the memory, Moscow has reason to be wary of creating de facto private armies or militias. At the same time, Russia’s military does not have the capacity to permanently protect every critical site, including power stations, airports, refineries and other industrial facilities.

The result is an increasingly distributed approach in which critical-infrastructure operators can provide some of the personnel, equipment and funding needed to protect their own facilities, while the state retains control over the wider air-defence architecture.

Also read: How vulnerable are airports to rogue drones? Also read: How vulnerable are airports to rogue drones?

France and Poland moving ahead with arming private companies

In August, France passed a law allowing operators of critical infrastructure and contractors to detect, jam, and shoot down drones near designated facilities.

France was spurred by a wave of drone incursions, including over its Île Longue nuclear submarine base late last year. Now France wants an updated list of sensitive sites vital to national security to be equipped with counter-drone systems by 2027. Details have not yet been made public.

For Germany, the discovery of the explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian An-124 at Leipzig/Halle Airport this August was another wake-up call.

In Germany, counter-UAS remains a policing function, although it is now reviewing how critical infrastructure operators and third parties could get involved in countering drones.

Reuters notes that Poland, sitting much closer to the frontline, has gone further than many European states. Operators of critical infrastructure said they have deployed countermeasures and are training with the Polish military and police.

Counter-drone measures are becoming increasingly automated, as it isn’t feasible to permanently establish manned fire teams to protect all critical infrastructure points.

]]> Pratt & Whitney unveils secretive new PT9 turboprop after five years of secret development https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/pratt-whitney-canada-pt9-turboprop/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 09:59:14 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54190 Pratt & Whitney Canada has surprised the industry with the launch of its all-new PT9 turboprop, revealing that the engine is already certified and designed to support future hybrid-electric propulsion architectures.

The post Pratt & Whitney unveils secretive new PT9 turboprop after five years of secret development appeared first on AGN.

]]> Pratt & Whitney Canada (part of RTX) has unexpectedly unveiled the PT9, an all-new turboprop engine that was developed largely out of public view and certified by Transport Canada before its official launch.

The engine features modern architecture with space for continuous improvement and integration into future electric and hybrid aircraft.

PW Canada has long dominated the turboprop market with its highly successful PT6 family, first introduced in the 1960s, and its larger PW100 series. Variants of those engines power anything from a Cessna Caravan to regional airliners.

PW Canada unveiled new cleansheet turboprop engine

Yesterday, at the NBAA-BACE business aviation show in Las Vegas, Pratt & Whitney Canada made a surprise revelation. It unveiled its latest turboprop engine, the PT9, with a “new centerline,” aka a cleansheet engine.

The engine has already accumulated more than 14,000 development hours and has been recently certified by Transport Canada.

Satheeshkumar Kumarasingam, president of Pratt & Whitney Canada, stated, “The PT9 engine represents the next evolution of turboprop propulsion, delivering significant advances in performance, efficiency and adaptability to meet the needs of modern aviation.”

He then explained the engine is designed around changing customer needs, including advanced digital capabilities and “future-ready hybridization.”

The company president said PT6’s architecture can be tailored to diverse airframe types while providing a “strong foundation” for more development.

PW’s new turboprop engine

PW claims it delivers 33% more power at altitude, while also reducing fuel consumption by 20% compared with previous-generation engines.

The PT9 is a completely new clean-sheet turboprop engine in the roughly 1,700–2,300 shaft horsepower class. It occupies the power gap between the upper end of the PT6 range and the lower end of the PW100 family.

Pratt didn’t name an aircraft it is intended for, but rather said it is suitable for “diverse airframe types.”

#NEWS: Pratt & Whitney Canada introduces certified PT9 engine, a new centerline turboprop delivering more power, efficiency and flexibility for next-generation aircraft. MORE: https://t.co/3yEFfGfcZe https://t.co/wuT0a7DpHM

— RTX (@RTX_News) October 21, 2026

PT9 is designed to combine the jet-like performance with turboprop efficiency while also incorporating next-generation architecture to allow its future evolution.

Pratt claims the engine’s modular design sets a foundation for continued innovation and technology integration. Future variants may power electric aircraft and hybrid thermal-electric powerplants.

Pratt & Whitney receives certification for 200th engine Pratt & Whitney receives certification for 200th engine

The surprise announcement and secret development

Yesterday’s announcement came as a surprise to many, catching the industry off-guard.

After decades of refining the legendary PT6, Pratt quietly built and certified the PT9. It is highly unusual for engines to be unveiled after receiving certification and being essentially “ready for the market.”

The programme’s five-year development was kept largely under wraps, with only faint hints appearing in the 2025 FAA regulatory filings (referring to a “PT9A-11” new-centerline turboprop).

It is also the first all-new turboprop in decades and is a noted departure from the familiar incremental PT6 upgrades. All-new engines are comparatively rare in the industry as they are expensive and time-consuming.

The engine’s debut comes as GE Aerospace is seeking to start challenging Pratt’s with its Catalyst turboprop and other engines.

]]> SyberJet SJ36 mock-up makes world debut at NBAA-BACE, as SJ34 deliveries targeted for 2029 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/syberjet-sj36-mockup-showcases-sj34-business-jet-nbaa/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 08:35:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54142 SyberJet has unveiled a mock-up of its SJ36 as it targets 2032 delivery date for its 8-passenger business jet, while first deliveries of its SJ34 are targeted for 2029.

The post SyberJet SJ36 mock-up makes world debut at NBAA-BACE, as SJ34 deliveries targeted for 2029 appeared first on AGN.

]]> US business jet manufacturer SyberJet is targeting the light jet market with two upgraded aircraft, promising transcontinental range, higher speeds and lower operational costs.

SyberJet unveiled a full-scale mock-up of its next-generation SJ36 business jet and outlined plans to bring its SJ34 to market, with reservations now being taken for both jets. The company is targeting the competitive light business jet sector with its two new airframes.

The manufacturer made the announcements at SyberJet World, Henderson Executive Airport in Las Vegas, on 19 November, on the eve of this year’s National Business Aviation Association (NBAA) Business Aviation Convention and Exhibition (BACE).

The company livestreamed the unveiling internationally and also showcased its proprietary SyberVision avionics suite, opening reservations for the SJ36.

SyberJet’s SJ36 targets light business jet sector

Designed to combine the speed and range traditionally associated with larger business jets, the SJ36 will also deliver the operating economics of a light jet. SyberJet is targeting a maximum operating speed of Mach 0.88, a range of up to 3,000nm and sea-level cabin pressure at altitudes of up to 41,000 ft.

The aircraft is an evolution of the manufacturer’s SJ30 platform, for which development was halted in the early 1990s when financial support was withdrawn. The SJ36 features a stretched fuselage, larger cabin, and upgraded systems. The single-pilot jet will accommodate up to eight passengers, positioning it for long domestic and transcontinental journeys.  

“This isn’t an incremental improvement – it’s a fundamental course change,” said Trevor Milton, CEO of SyberJet Aircraft.

A fixed-wing and rotorcraft pilot, Milton underlined the aircraft could offer a viable alternative to more expensive midsize jets for operators requiring longer-range capability.

“You no longer need a US$100,000 midsize charter to fly coast to coast – the SJ36 can do it for 50 to 70% less.”

It’s worth noting, however, that these savings are a company projection and will depend on the aircraft’s eventual acquisition price, operating costs and mission profile.

How SyberJet’s SJ36 is challenging established light jets.

Once it achieves and certifies its projected performance, the SJ36 could offer an alternative to established light business jets such as the Embraer Phenom 300E and Cessna Citation CJ4 Gen2. Its targeted range and cabin-pressure performance could also appeal to buyers who might otherwise consider midsize jets for longer journeys.

The aircraft’s proposed range of 3,000nm would also give it a significant reach advantage over many traditional light jets. Meanwhile, the target speed of Mach 0.88 would put it among the faster aircraft in its intended market.

While the SJ36 remains a development programme, SyberJet is confident of making first deliveries in 2032.

SyberJet’s SJ34 to succeed the SJ30-2

Alongside the SJ36, SyberJet outlined plans for its SJ34, which will replace the FAA-certified SJ30-2 and for which it is also now taking reservations.

The single-pilot jet is expected to accommodate up to six-passengers. It will retain the high-speed, long-range characteristics of the existing platform but will be upgraded with SyberVision avionics and larger Williams engines.

The SJ34 is expected to offer a range of up to 2,500nm and a maximum operating speed of Mach 0.83. The larger engines will deliver between 5,000 and 6,400 lbs of thrust, while the all-new interior will match the SJ36. First customer deliveries are expected in 2029.

The SJ34 is being offered to Passage One programme members at a launch price of US$10m, compared with the standard price of US$12 million.

New avionics at the centre of SyberJet’s programme

Both jets will feature SyberVision, the company’s proprietary avionics platform, which is expected to improve flight-deck integration, connectivity and pilot workflow. It includes six high-definition touchscreen displays, an integrated flight management system, secure over-the-air software updates and smartphone connectivity.

The company is also developing features including SyberPilot, described as an AI-assisted flight technology, alongside digital charting and improved taxi functions.

Connected features are intended to enable pilots to upload flight plans and access aircraft functions remotely, including cabin-temperature controls SyberJet is also promising a more premium passenger experience, with Italian leather seating and updated cabin systems.

Early access to SyberJet’s SJ36 and SJ34 to stimulate demand

SyberJet is offering early buyers access to its Passage One programme, which is limited to the first 250 customers. Members are being offered the stated launch prices of US$14m for the SJ36 and US$10m for the SJ34, a discount of US$2m from the respective standard prices of US$16m and US$12m announced by the company.

The programme is intended to attract early commitments as SyberJet looks to build demand ahead of production.

The challenge now is execution. The SJ36’s targeted range and speed make it an ambitious entrant into a market already served by established manufacturers. Meanwhile, the SJ34 must demonstrate that its upgrades translate into a compelling proposition against newer-generation light jets.

Milton remains hopeful: “We didn’t just show up at NBAA; we showed up having broken the world speed record for light jets by a whopping 48%. The full-scale SJ36 mock-up represents what the production aircraft is expected to look like. The avionics are world-class and may be better than any system on the market.”

For SyberJet’s Passage One Program members, Milton said customers could “save millions of dollars over the competition.” The exclusive club limited to the first 250 customers will include a SJ36 launch price of US$14m, instead of US$16m and an SJ34 launch price of US$10m instead of US$12m.

]]> Airlines fly Riyadh passengers to an airport four hours away as the capital’s flight disruption continues https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/riyadh-flights-al-qassim-airport-bus-transfers/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 07:41:20 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54164 Saudia and Riyadh Air are flying disrupted Riyadh passengers to Al Qassim Airport before transferring them by road to the Saudi capital as restrictions remain in place at King Khalid International Airport.

The post Airlines fly Riyadh passengers to an airport four hours away as the capital’s flight disruption continues appeared first on AGN.

]]> Saudia and Riyadh Air are rerouting passengers travelling to Riyadh through Al Qassim Airport, hundreds of kilometres from the Saudi capital, with onward road journeys taking over four hours.

Restrictions remain in place at King Khalid International Airport following missile and drone attacks earlier this month.

Saudia is offering passengers flights to Al Qassim, followed by road transfers to Riyadh. Riyadh Air is making similar arrangements for travellers affected by the disruption.

Al Qassim’s Prince Naif bin Abdulaziz International Airport, near Buraydah, is 375km by road from Riyadh.

This road transfer allows airlines to transport passengers to Riyadh without operating directly into King Khalid International Airport, which reopened on 18 October but remains subject to operational restrictions.

Also read: Is Riyadh airport open for international flights? Latest restrictions explained Also read: Is Riyadh airport open for international flights? Latest restrictions explained

Riyadh Air schedules special flights via Al Qassim Airport

Riyadh Air has arranged special flights from London Heathrow, Madrid and Bangkok to Al Qassim on Thursday, 22 October, to bring passengers affected by the disruption back to Saudi Arabia.

According to flight information published by Wego on 21 October, the planned services are:

All times are local. Services remain subject to operational changes.

Passengers arriving at Al Qassim will be transferred to Riyadh by complimentary bus. The transfer is included with the flight ticket and requires no separate reservation.

The special flights don’t constitute a resumption of Riyadh Air’s normal services to the capital. The airline continues to adjust its operations following the attacks.

Why are airlines using Al Qassim instead of Riyadh airport?

King Khalid International Airport has partially reopened, but airlines cannot yet operate unrestricted services.

As AGN has previously reported, two aviation notices took effect on 17 October.

NOTAM A3650/26 requires aircraft operators to obtain prior permission from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) before landing or departing. A second notice, A3651/26, prevents airlines from using Riyadh as a planned diversion airport.

Airlines must also consider the continuing security situation, aircraft availability and the practical difficulties of restoring schedules after an extended shutdown.

Al Qassim provides an alternative within Saudi Arabia, allowing passengers to complete the final part of their journey by road rather than waiting for normal services to resume at Riyadh.

Other Saudi airports have also been used to accommodate diverted flights. Saudia has rerouted some passengers through Dammam and Jeddah. flynas has adjusted services across its domestic network.

King Fahd Airport attack adds to Saudi aviation disruption

King Fahd Airport in Dammam suffered an attack late Wednesday evening, which killed one and injured eight others. The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the attack and halted operations at the airport. 

Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority reporting an attack late Wednesday evening on King Fahd Airport in Dammam has killed one and injured eight others.  Operations at the airport have been halted since approximately 23:15 local time. https://t.co/iIMzYss8sl https://t.co/pMsodunc8k

— Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) October 21, 2026

Limited flights resume at Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport

The Associated Press reported on 21 October that a limited number of Saudi airline flights had operated into and out of Riyadh, including services by Saudia and flynas. This is consistent with Flightradar24 data, which shows some Saudia and flynas flights on the schedule.  

The airport closed after repeated attacks began on 9 October. The strikes damaged airport facilities and commercial aircraft, including a Saudia Airbus A320 and a Riyadh Air Boeing 787.

Six aircraft sustained damage with a combined insured value of approximately $375 million. 

Airlines also moved aircraft away from Riyadh to reduce their exposure to further attacks.

Also read: Riyadh Airport is open again, but what does that actually mean for passengers? Also read: Riyadh Airport is open again, but what does that actually mean for passengers?

The disruption has continued despite the airport’s partial reopening. Lufthansa, KLM, Air France and several Asian and Gulf carriers have extended their flight suspensions.

Airlines have postponed service resumption, and some service suspensions extend into next year.

Passengers travelling to Riyadh should expect delays and longer journeys

Passengers with plans to fly to Riyadh should check their flight status. Those rerouted through Al Qassim should allow additional time for the bus transfer, which can take four to five hours depending on traffic.

Riyadh Air is offering affected passengers the option to rebook eligible journeys without a change fee or request a refund, according to its official travel advisory.

The airline has not announced when its full schedule at King Khalid International Airport will resume.

For now, some passengers travelling to Saudi Arabia’s capital will arrive several hundred kilometres short of Riyadh and continue by road.

}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}
/* Hover-gap fix: invisible bridge spanning the 6px gap between the nav item
 and the dropdown panel, so the cursor never "leaves" while crossing. */
.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {

 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}

 first paint — each component's .open/.is-open rules override these. */
.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;

 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;

 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);

 border-top-left-radius: 22px;

 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {

 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;

 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;

 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;

 color: #0b3770;

 border-radius: 8px;

 flex-shrink: 0;

 }

 .sie-dest-panel__card {

 background: #1d3557;

 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );

 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,

 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>

</ul>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/the-effective-management-and-ownership-of-erasmus-for-internationalisation" target="_blank">The effective management and ownership of Erasmus +’ for ‘internationalisation’</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/internationalisation-at-the-university-of-helsinki" target="_blank">Internationalisation at the University of Helsinki </a></div>
                                             </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close-text"><i class="fa fa-times fa-2x"></i><span>Close</span></div>
                </div>
            </div>
                         <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q2.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
